speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, November 14, 1983 consideration of the motion of Mr. De Bane that Bill C-170, an Act to authorize investment in and the provision of financial assistance to the Atlantic Fisheries for the purpose of restructuring certain fishery enterprises, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to support Bill C-170. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) deserves the lion's share of credit for the initiative which is contained in this Bill. He, together with many others, has worked over many months to come up with the set of arrangements which are now before the House. I commend him and the many others who were involved, including the Premier of Newfoundland, Mr. Peckford, for the excellent results which have been achieved.
The deep sea sector of the fishery is the very cornerstone of the fishing industry in Atlantic Canada. I have some related figures, Mr. Speaker, which will show you what 1 mean. In 1982 there were sales of just over three quarters of a billion dollars, $770 million. And that was in a year when the industry was not in full swing. Indeed, some of the fish plants had been obliged to close late in that year, August and September, for various reasons, including financial ones. Notwithstanding, there were sales of more than three quarters of a billion dollars, which meant that 44,000 people in Atlantic Canada were employed in the deep sea sector. There were
20,000	fishermen, either in small boats, which in effect commute to fishing areas every day, or in trawlers and draggers, which go further afield and return home every few days with the catch.
[DOT]	(UlO)
There are 20,000 people in that category, another 24,000 men and women who depend directly on the fish processing plants in Atlantic Canada, a total of 44,000 people depending on this part of the fishery alone. When you relate those figures
to the population of Atlantic Canada, Mr. Speaker, you see how significant the deep sea fishing activity is to the economy of the region. It is fair to say that, in relative terms, the deep sea fishery is as significant to Atlantic Canada as is the automobile industry to central Canada. For that reason alone, letting the deep sea fishery go under is unthinkable.
That was one of the options, Mr. Speaker, one I thought was academic and to be dismissed out of hand until 1 heard continuing and disturbing suggestions that somehow the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, the Government of Nova Scotia and the Government of Canada ought not to be involved in this exercise. If you accept the argument that those three Governments ought not to be involved, you must ask the question: What then happens without the involvement of those three Governments? 1 would suggest one of two things: either the industry goes under completely, a complete collapse of the deep sea sector and the resulting chaos for three, four or five years until someone comes in and picks up the pieces; or we could have Government involvement in another way, as we have had over the years, that which I choose to characterize as the band-aid approach where we throw good money after bad by giving taxpayers' money to fish company managers to manage as badly as they have managed their own money.
There were, Mr. Speaker, just three options: to continue applying for band-aids; to walk away from the problem and allow economic and social chaos of a substantial size; or to do what is being proposed in this legislation. I support wholeheartedly the approach taken in this legislation, having in mind that I represent the largest fishing riding in all of Canada. I represent 1,500 miles of coastline with 135 communities, almost all of which have a very direct relationship to the fishery, many of them to the deep sea sector.
By way of example, there are 12 so-called deep sea plants in Newfoundland, eight of them in the riding of Burin-St. George's. Those plants are at Burgeo, Ramea, Gaultois, Harbour Breton, Grand Bank, Fortune, Marystown and Burin. In addition to those eight plants there are another 14, for a total of 22, in the riding of Burin-St. George's which depend on the fishery.
It would be helpful if we tried to put a human face on what we are talking about. Let us look at a community such as Ramea. This is a community of 1,400 people located on an island a few miles off the south coast of the island of Newfoundland. One hundred and twenty-five people of the community work the boats, either the trawlers or the inshore, and another 300 or so work in the plant. With fishermen and fish plant workers together there are 450 people out of 1,400 who

November 17, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act depend directly on the fishing industry for employment. One out of every three people in that community are directly employed in the fishery. For them the choice is not between fishing and some other employment activity. The choice is between fishing and nothing. The choice is between having a job in the fishery and seeing their employment opportunity, community and whole lifestyle collapse. That is Ramea.
I could mention Gaultois, which is also on an island and depends on a fish plant for its employment. 1 could mention Harbour Breton. I could mention some of the inshore communities like McCallum, Franpois, Grey River, Grand Bruit and La Poile. These communities know only one way of life. It is a way of life that has served them very well. If you are looking for record crime rates you do not look to these communities. If you are looking for vagrancy and vandalism you do not look to these communities. These phenomena are almost foreign to the very proud and dignified way of life which the people in those communities pursue. I for one want to see to it that we in this House do everything within our power to ensure that that way of life is allowed to continue, is encouraged and is allowed to enhance itself. Canada is well served by people of that ilk. Canada is well served by people with a value system such as we find alive, well and thriving in communities such as I have mentioned.
This Bill does not seek to make welfare ghettos of those communities, Mr. Speaker, but to allow them to continue a profitable economic activity which they have pursued with vigour over the years and still want to pursue. The only reason they have not been able to do it unimpeded is that we have had some fish company managers who have let their enthusiasm get in the way of their judgment. They have allowed those deep sea companies to become overextended financially and generally have made some other incompetent, ill-advised decisions, financial and otherwise.
The consequence is that we have an industry with much potential. After all, if you cannot make money selling fish in today's world, what can you make money at? The potential is there and has always been there. The independents are proving that so well. Even in very hard times the so-called independents in my riding are doing very well at a time when they had many adverse factors with which to contend. They continue to sell their fish. They continue to make a dollar.
[DOT] (U20)
The same could have been the case with the deep sea sector, if we did not have some overenthusiastic fish company managers who made some terribly incompetent decisions. Our time is being taken up here today because of the chaotic, disastrous results of those incompetent decisions.
In this Bill, the Government of Canada, in collaboration with the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador and the Government of Nova Scotia, proposes the only sensible course of action open to it. A couple of days ago I listened with some interest to my good friend from South Shore (Mr. Crouse), in Nova Scotia, who spoke in this debate. Among other things, he suggested that a thorough search of the private sector has not
been done in an effort to find investment capital. I respect his view, and that may well be his view, but I submit to him that it is a very wrong view.
I do not ask him to accept my version on my say so, but before he makes that kind of statement publicly I ask him to compare notes with a colleague from his own Party, the Premier of Newfoundland. It is no secret to the House that the Premier of Newfoundland wanted very much to get the deep sea sector back on a stable footing without the involvement of the Government of Canada. The Premier of Newfoundland did everything he possibly could to attract private capital. His exploits to find private capital on both sides of the Atlantic are well known. He did everything within his power to try to find private capital. The principals of Fisheries Products also did everything within their power to find private capital, as did the Canadian Development Corporation and the Bank of Nova Scotia. Therefore I believe it is somewhat misleading for the hon. gentleman from South Shore to say that there is private capital out there.
Let me put it differently. If he knows of private capital which is out there, let him tell the House and the Government. I make an undertaking to him now that if he can come forward with the private capital we will scrap this Bill. We will do away with it because there will be no need for it.
The reason this legislation is before us today is that all Parties involved, the Government of Newfoundland, the companies concerned and the other investors, have all failed in the most diligent effort to find private capital to stabilize this deep sea sector. The gentleman from South Shore wants a schedule by which the Government would divest itself of the shares. I believe he has a schedule. I believe he has a firm undertaking from the Government and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans as well as the Premier of Newfoundland that the divestiture will take place at the earliest possible opportunity. If a buyer shows up reasonably soon, the shareholders provided for in this legislation will be very happy to talk to that buyer on an urgent basis.
I always become a little amused when I hear the Tories talking about the socialist umbrella, as the gentleman from the South Shore characterized it. I do not know where that leaves the Premier of Newfoundland, because he is part of this same so-called umbrella, or where it leaves Premier Buchanan of Nova Scotia. 1 never thought of him as being a socialist. 1 suppose it is the same old story in which the Tories stand for many things. They stand for one thing in this Chamber, something else in the hustings, something else in the Government of Nova Scotia and something else in the Government of Newfoundland. It must be very convenient to talk out of all sides of one's mouth at the same time.
This legislation has nothing to do with socialism. It has to do with a pragmatic approach. It has to do with responsibility. It has to do with doing what has to be done. The alternative is to allow those thousands of jobs to go down the drain.
November 17, 1983

Let us make up our minds. Which is it? Is it some sinister approach which the gentleman from South Shore would have us believe? Or is it, as the Premier of Newfoundland, another great Tory, says-the best thing that happened to Newfoundland since Confederation? Which is it? Is it good or is it sinister? The economic viability of the industry must be the ultimate objective.
We have tempered that objective, of course, with a social cabinet. We recognize that communities such as Ramea, Gaul-tois, St. Anthony and Harbour Breton would have no future outside the fishery. So the Government has said that in those cases the industry ought not to bear the financial brunt. The Government of Canada on behalf of the taxpayers ought to address that issue. If it is determined that it is in the best interests to put taxpayers' money into communities like Ramea, the Government will do it quite apart from any objectives of the company which will manage the industry.
Finally, the question arises: Do I, as the Member who represents the largest fishing riding in Canada, have some reservations about this particular Bill? As a matter of fact, I do. It is not a perfect document. It is the result of a set of compromises which have been worked out with all the Parties involved.
Allow me, then, to state one of my reservations. This Bill has the effect of taking the Bank of Nova Scotia off the hook. I do not like that and I do not care who knows that I do not like it. The bank does not deserve to be taken off the hook. When the bank advanced the credit, it took its chances, or so you would believe. When the day of reckoning came, the bank should have lost its shirt for aiding and abetting incompetent fish company managers for making incompetent financial decisions. But that is not what happened; the bank did not lose its shirt because it had an ace up its sleeve. It had the Government across a barrel, in effect. It knew Governments would not stand by and allow bankruptcies to proceed and the assets of the deep sea sector dismantled and auctioned off. That would have put the industry in chaos for three to five years. The bankers sat in Toronto and smiled, and well they might. Their no lose scenario was working to perfection. Taxpayers would once again bail them out. At the right time we have to address that issue. We have to rein in those bankers so that they serve the people of this country instead of abusing them. This is the place, but this is not the time.
Let me say in conclusion that whiie I have some very serious reservations about the role of the bankers in this field, 1 recognize the Governments involved are doing the only thing they can to salvage the situation. It will do more than salvage; it will stabilize the situation and make for a very profitable fishery in the years ahead in Newfoundland and Atlantic Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking on this Bill, I must point out that it is a very sketchy and incompetent piece of legislation that we are asked to approve by the Government opposite. This Bill does not in any way explain to us how the Government plans to carry out the so-called restructuring of the fishing industry in Canada.
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
The Minister when he introduced the Bill, as reported at page 28848 of Hansard, asked the question:
How can an industry that has so much going for it manage to get itself into such serious trouble?
The Minister went on and introduced the Bill but never once answered that question. There has been no rational explanation by the Government as to how the East Coast Atlantic fishery got into the state it is now in. The Minister has not explained whether or not this has anything to do with the policies of the federal Government. The fishery is solely within the jurisdiction of the Government of Canada. The Minister has not explained what policies of the federal Government might have contributed to the debacle in the fishing industry off the East Coast of Canada. He has not explained to this House how these policies will be changed or what new policies there will be that might change the situation.
His introduction of the Bill was full of half-truths and specious reasoning. The Minister said that the agreements reached with Newfoundland and Nova Scotia reflected to some extent the recommendations made by the Kirby task force. 1 do not know to what extent this Bill and these restructuring agreements agree with the report of the task force. They appear to be diametrically opposed. There was great conflict between the Kirby task force and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane). The recommendations of the task force are not carried out in the Bill. In fact, it does not even refer to the restructuring agreement entered into with Newfoundland or with Nova Scotia.
Then the Minister went on to say that the industry needed to become leaner and more efficient ashore and afloat. How will the industry become leaner and more efficient ashore and afloat if the Bill is passed? If Government-controlled corporations are to take over the industry in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, is it likely that there will be a leaner and more efficient structure, especially when a government or two governments are involved? Of course not. In my view, unfortunately we will see a Canadair applied to the fishing industry. There will be a great deal of losses in these new companies. They will not be leaner and more efficient. Once the politicians are involved, they will be anything but lean and efficient.
The Minister claimed that he reached an agreement with the Governments of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. He has not reached an agreement with the Government of Nova Scotia. There is a so-called agreement in principle, but there is no other agreement with Nova Scotia. He said that it was an agreement in principle. That is all it is.
There was no explanation by the Minister of why we should approve the Bill and no suggestion as to how it should be improved. There is no accountability under this piece of legislation. It is inadequate, disappointing, frightening and irresponsible. The legislation authorizes the Government to make loans, to give guarantees or to give grants to any fishing company or fishing arrangement that it wishes. It does not have to report back to the House as to whom it has made the

November 17, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act loans, to whom it has given the grants or why. It does not have to report annually to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry as to what it has done, why, to whom it has done it or how much money it has spent. The Government asks us to approve $138 million to be spent between now and March 31, 1985, without its having any obligation to return and report to the House.
We just listened to the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons) trying to blame the position of the industry on incompetent decisions by fish plant managers. What absolute tripe, to blame fish plant managers! What caused the crisis in the fishing industry? It was not the Bank of Nova Scotia which caused it. The Bank of Nova Scotia, poor devils, tried to support the fishing industry down through the years. They made loans and did their best to carry the fishing industry until it got beyond them. Why did it get beyond them? It was because of the interest rate structure in Canada. This incompetent Government which sits opposite allowed interest rates to rise to 22 per cent and 23 per cent. Today the rates are still 14 per cent or 15 per cent for companies engaged in the fishing industry.
This industry has very little equity in it. It has always been undercapitalized, has always had to borrow money and go to the banks to be supported. That is the history of the East Coast fishery. There has been heavy participation by the banks in the fishery. The banks and entrepreneurs took risks. Then this incompetent Government allowed the interest rate to go to 23 per cent, wrecked those fishing enterprises and made it no longer possible for the banks to carry the industry; the only alternative was for the Government to step in and carry it. There was no mention of that by the specious Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's. It has nothing to do with fish plant managers. The Hon. Member said that they overexpended. If the fishing companies overexpended, it was because they were encouraged to overexpend by the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's, by politicians and by Governments generally. It was because DREE made grants and loans available, as did the provincial Governments.
Another reason the fishing industry is in its present position is overcapacity, but the main reasons are high interest rates and lack of equity, as well as marketing problems. The Minister did not explain that National Sea has had to close its plants in Newfoundland, not because of overexpansion or incompetent decisions of fish plant managers, but because it could not sell the product. The situation in the market for frozen fish products in the last year or two has been difficult because of the recession and competition from other products such as turkey, chicken and the like. National Sea has had to close at Burgeo and St. John's because of these marketing problems.
The Hon. Member did not explain that a lot of the trouble was caused by lack of sufficient throughput; many plants do not have sufficient fish to put through to keep the plants operating for a long enough period to meet overhead costs. Sufficient fish are not being caught to go through those plants. That is the responsibility of the Government of Canada. The Government of Canada decides on quotas and allocates quotas.
The federal Government of Canada is largely responsible, 1 would say to a degree of at least 90 per cent, for the crisis in the East Coast fishing industry. That is why it is the Government's obligation to bring in a measure to help it. Unfortunately the only alternative it is offering is the Bill now before the House.
We have no option but to support the Bill now before us. How could we stand by and see the East Coast fishing industry, the offshore fishing industry, collapse? In my own district of St. John's West there are 23 fish plants. One major plant is the National Sea plant with six stern trawlers. It is closed today; it has been closed for several months. It employs 400 or 500 people. There is the major fish plant at Trepassey of Fishery Products Limited with five stern trawlers. It has been closed for the last two or three months. It employs 500 or 600 people. There are three inshore plants at Petty Harbour. At Bay Bulls there is a major inshore plant. Unfortunately it was just destroyed by fire. The O'Briens, a tremendous force in the Newfoundland inshore fishery, are hoping to rebuild. Witless Bay has an inshore plant. There are plants at Tor's Cove, Calvert-the Ferryland saltfish operation-Aquaforte and Fermeuse. The plant at Fermeuse is a major one which used to be supplied by offshore as well as inshore vessels. Now it is to be restricted to an inshore operation. Also there are the ones at St. Marys, Riverhead, Jersey Side, Argentia, Branch, St. Bride's, Little Harbour East, Fairhaven and Arnold's Cove. It is a major National Sea plant with only a few workers today; normally there are 300. Also there is the Admiral's Cove inshore plant and one at Southern Harbour. Of 23 fish plants, all of them are closed today with the exception of Arnold's Cove which has a few workers. Twenty are principally involved in the cod fishery, one operation for crab only and two for saltfish only. Naturally I will support the Bill. What alternative do I have? We cannot continue to have all those plants shut.
There are other problems upon which the Minister did not touch. He did not explain when he would start the resource-short fishing program to assist inshore plants. "The resource-short plant program", they so grandly call it. I have a telegram to the Minister from the community of Fermeuse asking when he would carry out his promise in the agreement signed in Newfoundland on September 26 to allocate fish to Fermeuse under the resource-short plant program. When will he get that off the ground? Canadian trawler operators have offered to catch offshore fish and sell it to inshore operators at cost. Inshore plant operators say that they cannot afford to pay that cost. There is a stalemate. The plants are still closed and people are still unemployed. The Minister does not seem to be bothered about it. He does not seem to be agitated about it. He did not mention it when he introduced this legislation to the House a few days ago.
If there can be no agreement between plant operators and Canadian trawler operators, and if it is possible for inshore plant operators to make a deal with foreign-owned fishing operators for this year, why not let it go ahead? If that is the only way plants like the one at Fermeuse can start to operate
November 17, 1983

again-and I have forgotten for exactly how long it has been closed; probably a year-then I suggest and recommend to the Minister that he arrange a deal and allow foreign-owned vessels to be used this year to catch the fish and get those plants operating again.
What we are being asked for in this Bill is to give the Government carte blanche, a blank cheque to intervene in the fisheries as it likes by way of loan guarantees or grants. That is what we are being asked to do. Having helped to bring about the collapse of the Canadian East Coast fishery, it is certainly questionable whether the Government of Canada has the competence to restore the East Coast fishery to economic viability. What has the Minister said that indicates to us that the Government is going to restore economic viability in the fishery? What is it going to bring to the fishery other than an unlimited supply of public funds?
What does the Government have to offer except public money? It has not shown us how it will make this industry lean and efficient or how the independent fish processor will be protected. It has shown us nothing, yet it asks us for a blank cheque. This legislation should be amended so that they have to report back to this House through the fisheries committee each year exactly what moneys have been spent under the legislation, who have been given guarantees and loans and just what is happening.
There is a vital inconsistency in the various clauses of the Bill. I quote two of the objectives:
-first, that the Atlantic fishing industry be economically viable on an on-going basis, second, that employment in that industry be maximized subject to the constraint that those employed receive a reasonable income-
There is an inconsistency in that objective. To be economically viable and to maximize employment is the matter of contention that has been at issue between the Kirby task force and the Government ever since the Kirby task force reported. The Government has not accepted the Kirby task force because it cannot decide that question. The question is still undecided. It is before us in the agreements that have been signed with Newfoundland. That inconsistency still has not been settled.
It is not with any great sense of elation that I have reluctantly concluded that we have to accept this Bill. It is only because nothing better has been put before us. The Minister did not answer any questions on the important issue. The Government is trying to press us to pass this Bill without any discussion in the House or in committee, although it was on July 2 that the Minister announced he was going ahead with this scheme. It was on September 26, two months ago, that the agreement was signed with Newfoundland. This Bill was only put before the House on October 31. We are being asked to rush it through in 24 hours even though the Government has bungled this problem for over a year.
Some of the questions the Minister should answer either in committee or in the House when the Bill returns are as follows: How is the Government going to assist the independents and
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act keep them involved in the fishery? They are discouraged and now want to get out. We have the statement of Alphonsus Best of Southern Harbour, the President of the independents' association in Newfoundland. He says the Government may as well buy them out and take them over now; they cannot stand unfair competition which they feel they will have from the two giant Government-controlled corporations. The Minister did not touch on that.
What is the Minister going to do to protect us in the U.S. market from actions taken there in the nature of anti-dumping and restraint of trade? There will be countervailing tariff applications made in the United States. They will complain of unfair competition to U.S. fishermen from these Government-controlled and financed companies. What steps has the Minister taken to try and avoid that threat? What has he done in the United States to try and get around that major problem? What steps will he take in the future? There is a great danger of countervailing tariff action in the U.S. because of the so-called restructuring.
The Minister has not told us what decisions are going to be made about very delicate matters, such as who will be entitled to fish in the Gulf of St. Lawrence to catch the increased red fish stocks that are now supposedly present in the Gulf. In 1974-75, the Newfoundland and Nova Scotia trawlers as well as other trawlers were ordered not to fish in the Gulf until the red fish stocks came back.
The fish plants on the south coast taken over from the Lakes at Ramea, Burgeo, Gaultois, and Harbour Breton, need access to those stocks. That is why they were put there in the first place. As to the Nova Scotia vessels, is the Government going to permit trawlers to re-enter and fish in the Gulf again for a certain quota of red fish or not?
What is to be the decision there? What does the Minister plan to do about that? How can this restructured company in Newfoundland be viable economically if it is not allowed to fish those stocks? The Minister should explain how they are going to be viable if they have to send their trawlers north off Labrador, even though they are not especially ice strengthened, at three or four times the cost and two or three times the danger? How will they have access to the fish stocks that will permit them to be lean, hungry and viable? The Minister has not even touched on that problem. What is he going to do about the unclear aims; economic efficiency and viability versus employment as well as Unemployment Insurance benefits or social considerations?
Who will be the directors? Will they be political hacks? Will it be Liberal hacks appointed by the Government, as is usually the case, or will they be independent-thinking people with some experience in business, law, the fishery or labour? What kind of people will be directors?
How can a miracleman be found who will be able to do all the inconsistent things he will have to do as managing director of one of those two huge companies? He will have to satisfy federal politicians, federal bureaucrats, provincial politicians and provincial bureaucrats. He will have to deal with his directors, the plant employees, inshore fishermen and trawler

November 17, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act fishermen. They all have inconsistent purposes. The interests of one are not necessarily the same as the interests of the other. How will he be able to run an efficient company, look after marketing, sales in the U.S. and the European Common Market as well as fish production? Where is such a superman to be found? He will have to look after the members of every fishing district which has a fish plant apart altogether from Governments. When are they going to find such a man?
These two companies have no financial plan for next year. They do not know what their budgets will be for next year. They do not know who will be in charge. Morale is shattered. The Minister has not spoken of all these problems. The Minister thinks all problems will be solved because the Government will put more money in and it will be a Government-controlled corporation. What is the fishing plan for those companies for next year? What quotas of fish stocks is the Minister assigning to those two companies for next year? There is total confusion. The Government bungled the attempt to get the shareholders out of the way of those companies. It took so long that it did tremendous damage to marketing in the United States in the case of Fishery Products Limited.
There was bungling with reference to the Government's own Canada Development Corporation, complete bungling. That company, which is 48 per cent owned by the Government, could not even discuss with the Government some sensible way to compensate them to get their shares and those of the Monroes. The Government had to be brought to its knees by court action taken in Canada and the United States. It was a complete bungling. The Minister should submit his resignation now because of the untold damage caused by the shareholders. What agreement has been reached with the shareholders? What is agreed to be paid to the CDC, the Monroes and the Lakes? The Minister has not given us any figure as to what happened there. I hope it will all be discussed and explained in committee.
How are they going to overcome the disruption in the U.S. markets? The fishery was better off when the entrepreneurs were in charge, risking their money, such as they had, and borrowing from the banks. They were hard workers and gamblers. I would like to say a kind word about them as they depart.
The Lakes, the Penneys, the Moores, the Russells, the Monroes, their replacements will be hard to find. It is never the same when you are dealing with somebody else's money. There is no bottom line. The Government is going to put in the money. If they lose $100 million this year, the Government will put in another $100 million next year. It is not hard to find people who do not mind spending other people's money. It is a far different breed that built up this industry. They risked their own money and the money they borrowed from the banks, only to be finally done in by an incompetent Government which allowed interest rates to go to 23 per cent.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. 1 regret to interrupt the Hon. Member but I must inform him that his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to ask the Hon. Member a question. Is the Hon. Member aware that the Premier of his own Province has publicly stated that this is the most beneficial action for his Province taken by the federal Government since Newfoundland's entry into Confederation in 1949? Second, is he aware that the Premier of his Province has just tabled in the Legislature of Newfoundland a Bill ratifying the agreement that we have signed and urging that it be passed unanimously?

Mr. Speaker, I am certainly aware that the Premier of the Province welcomed the fact that the Government of Canada had at last come to its senses and agreed to give the provincial Government some say in how the new company was to operate, and the Premier also welcomed the fact that the Minister had finally taken a more reasonable stand by dropping the position he had taken on July 2 and entering into an agreement that was more favourable to the provincial Government and would give it some say in the fishery. However, if the Premier ever said that this was the greatest thing since Confederation or sliced bread, then I would only have to say to the Minister that 1 do not agree with him.
I think that this action will stave off the complete collapse of the fishery industry but it is the only alternative that is presented to us. The only alternative to the collapse of the fishery industry is a blank cheque which the Government will now give these companies in order to save the industry for a while. However, I do not say that this is the greatest thing since sliced bread. I have not seen any plan presented by the Minister that would show us how this will result in any benefit other than to keep fish plants open at the moment. It is a confession of abject failure on behalf of the Minister.
The Premier of Newfoundland is pleased because the Government of Canada had to concede that the provincial Government should have some say over the operations of the company. Naturally he was pleased that the Minister dropped his previous stubborn and stupid attitude, but if the Premier said the words attributed to him by the Minister, then 1 would have to say that I do not agree. I think that this is a bad job that has been initiated by the Minister and his Government and we have no alternative but to support it and hail it. Other than on that basis, I would not agree with the Minister.
What was the second part of the Minister's question? The first part of his question was so jejune that I have forgotten the second part of his question.

Mr. Speaker, 1 listened with great interest to the speech made by the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). I am not an expert in this field and I do not represent very many fishermen, but some things seem to me to be pretty obvious from the reports we have had.
November 17, 1983

The fishing industry, which is one of the main industries in Atlantic Canada and employs tens of thousands of people, was operated for many years by private companies. For various reasons, some of which include overexpansion, high interest rates and cutbacks in the markets, the industry was going bankrupt. The banks could no longer carry the private industry.
That being the case, there was an agreement reached between the federal Liberal Government and at least two Conservative provincial Governments, the Government of Newfoundland and the Government of Nova Scotia. That agreement provided that the only way the industry could be saved and tens of thousands of people could be assisted was through massive Government intervention. That, Mr. Speaker, has been the history of so many industries in so many parts of Canada. The Government has intervened when the private sector could not do the job. This is not necessarily a criticism of the private sector, but that has been a fact of life.
The federal Liberal Government and the provincial Conservative Governments have reached an agreement. I am not competent to say whether that agreement is the best one that could have been reached or whether it will succeed, but surely it is obvious that the private sector did not and could not do the job. Yet it seems to me that the only solution which the Hon. Member for St. John's West has put forth as an alternative to what has been agreed on between the federal Liberal Government and the two provincial Conservative Governments is that somehow the Governments should give more money, either through grants or loans, to the private companies which have already failed. It seems to me that that is neither possible nor advisable.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for asking a sensible question. It is the only sensible question 1 have been asked this morning.
The situation is that this is not an industry like any other industry because the source of its raw material is controlled by the Government. The fishing industry is unlike the agricultural industry in which the farmer can decide how many turnips or how much wheat or whatever he will plant. The fish resources are common property resources controlled by the Government. As well, many other aspects of the industry are controlled by the Government, including the kind of boat that can be used, whether the fisherman can get a licence for a trawler, a 65-foot longliner or a trap skip, or whether he can fish at all. All of this is controlled and licensed by the Government, so we are not dealing with an ordinary industry.
We are dealing with an industry in eastern Canada which, because there are no large amounts of capital available to be invested, has always been undercapitalized while its equipment is becoming more and more expensive. It does not represent the normal industrial situation. The responsibility for what has happened in the fishery industry is, to a major degree, that of the Government itself because of some of those factors I have mentioned.
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
With respect to the two Conservative Governments, the Government of Nova Scotia itself has not yet reached any agreement with the federal Government except for a so-called agreement in principle. The details of that agreement which are more important than its principle have not been agreed upon.
The Government of Newfoundland had no choice but to accept an agreement that would give it some say in what would happen. Newfoundland is a Province in which the fishery industry is the most important of its industries and is the biggest employer of its people. The only reason anyone lives in rural Newfoundland is to work in the fishery industry and the fishery industry is not controlled by the provincial Government at all. It is as if the land and the grain and everything in the Province of Saskatchewan were completely federally controlled.
From the point of view of the Government of Newfoundland, first the fishery industry had to be saved and rural Newfoundland had to be saved. That could only be done by the federal Government and if the provincial Government could get an agreement to give it some influence over the issues that are to be decided upon in the future, that would be an advantage. Finally, after getting that concession from the federal Government, it entered into an agreement to which it had no alternative in any event. We cannot have fish plants all over Newfoundland collapse, and if the only way to keep them going is through money from the federal Government, the provincial Government of Newfoundland naturally must support that, just as I must support it because there are 23 fish plants in my district.
Although 1 am supporting the agreement on that basis, Mr. Speaker, it does not mean that 1 believe it is the right solution. 1 myself would have preferred to see the Government allow the industry to continue in private hands but have the Government take over the plants that it wants to operate for social reasons and operate them itself separate from the other companies. Fishery Products Limited should not be operating a plant that it does not think is economical because that would give it an excuse to say in future years, if it has not done well, that it was prevented from doing so by the fact that it had operated plants that were uneconomical. Those plants should be taken over by the Government. If they are needed for social purposes, they should be operated by the Government.
The Government should have made financial arrangements through loans or, to some extent, grants to assist the trawler companies to continue in business because it was the Government's own economic policies and incompetence that put the fishing industry in a position where it could no longer survive and made it impossible for the Bank of Nova Scotia to continue its financing. That would have been my preferred solution, Mr. Speaker.

November 17, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

Mr. Speaker, I would say to the last speaker that perhaps his concern should have been made known to his own provincial Government before it went into the arrangement, because it is now a partner to an arrangement. At least we from Nova Scotia have only an agreement to co-operate between the two Governments.
Bill C-170 is an Act to authorize investment in and the provision of financial assistance to the Atlantic Fisheries for the purpose of restructuring certain fishery enterprises. It is by far the most important piece of legislation I have seen come before Parliament in the years in which I have represented South West Nova. It may not be the Constitution, the Crow Bill, any one of the budget Bills, or the six and five legislation, but to the people in the Atlantic Provinces this Bill will have a far-reaching effect. I believe that as politicians we must make sure that we get the most out of this Bill before it is passed in this House. Certainly my constituents feel it will affect them, and they want more information.
This legislation came about because of the Kirby task force. The powers the Bill gives to the Minister seem to be unlimited. The Kirby task force was established in January, 1982. It was to study the Atlantic coast fisheries and report to an ad hoc committee of Ministers on the Atlantic fisheries. In December of 1982 it made its recommendations on establishing and maintaining viable fishery enterprises on the Atlantic coast of Canada.
The Kirby task force set out three objectives which form the basis of its recommendations. I would like to quote from the Kirby task force report because I feel it is important for us to know the context in which we now have this Bill before us. At page VII the report lists three objectives in order of priority which should guide Atlantic fisheries policy. And remember, these are in order of priority:
Objective 1: The Atlantic fishing industry should be economically viable on an ongoing basis, where to be viable implies an ability to survive downturns with only a normal business failure rate and without government assistance.
That was the top priority. I will read the next two priorities:
Objective 2: Employment in the Atlantic fishing industry should be maximized subject to the constraint that those employed receive a reasonable income as a result of fishery-related activities, including fishery-related income transfer payments.
Objective 3: Fish within the 200-mile Canadian zone should be harvested and processed by Canadians in firms owned by Canadians wherever this is consistent with Objectives 1 and 2 and with Canada's international treaty obligations.
These objectives are important to remember because I feel that this Bill.and the restructuring of the fisheries seem to be in direct contradiction of these objectives, particularly the primary objective of economic viability.
Before commenting on the Bill itself, I would just like to go back a couple of years and review some of the history which brought about the Kirby task force, as well as the present
collapse of the five large fishing companies on the East Coast. This Bill, Mr. Speaker, does not seem to be taking history into account. What we saw happening in 1981 was that five large East Coast companies were holding inventories which were too high. This was mainly due to a softening in our existing markets. The East Coast fisheries had seen this happen before. In fact, the last time it happened was in 1973. In 1974-75 the federal Government put approximately $150 million into assisting these companies and their inventories. Again, at that time, Mr. Speaker, the markets were soft.
In late 1980 through 1981, with soft marketing conditions and increased fish landings, inventories were again high and the market price depressed. Fish inventories have always been financed by banks and in 1980 interest rates went up and continued to climb. The debt incurred to finance the inventories and to hold these inventories became too great for the companies and they came looking to the federal Government and to the provincial Governments, as well as to the banks, for financial assistance.
We also found at that time that we did not have any mechanism at the federal level to alleviate this problem. We had a fisheries prices support board which could only remove inventories and hold them at similar cost to the companies as that provided by the banks. The Government did not appear to have any ability to offer an outright purchase of the inventory and then try to resell it later when the market could take up the excess inventory, and thereby avoid dumping fish into soft markets at certainly lower prices.
The Government gave no financial guarantees to an industry which was the most important industry on the East Coast as far as employment and revenues were concerned. Some companies, in my view, might still be in existence had they been provided with some sort of assistance. Heaven knows, over the years federal Governments have assisted other operations in Canada, such as Massey-Ferguson, Canadair and Dome Petroleum, yet our basic resource industry got the Kirby task force.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, how will this Bill ensure orderly marketing when our marketing capabilities go soft? I have always felt that federal involvement, along with the provincial involvement-because the Provinces have the jurisdiction to market fish-should have been concentrated on establishing a voluntary orderly marketing program. Such a program would set up an organization which would be able to sell excess fish and not have to compete in an existing soft market. In other words, if there were high inventories these inventories could be removed at the wish of the company and sold into either new markets, which would have been established by some mechanism, or sold at a later date into the existing market when the market had hardened up.
Today we have before us a Bill which does not establish a voluntary marketing system on the East Coast. 1 must say that the Kirby task force does deal with marketing in great depth. However, this Bill does not mention any of this. In fact, the Minister stated in his speech on Monday that there would be three new marketing companies. Again, Mr. Speaker, are

these companies to compete among themselves and the smaller processors? Will they eventually have the same marketing conditions which have existed in the past, without any relief ?
My concern, Mr. Speaker, is that this Bill will set up and fund three super East Coast companies. It is a Bill which incorporates the exact amount of money needed to establish these three super companies and which, from what I have read, does not set up any financing for the small independent companies which may also be in trouble. This is a Bill which, in my view, does not even resemble the recommendations of the Kirby task force. We have in fact a Bill which talks about economic viability in the preamble, incorporating the primary recommendation of Kirby, but does not talk about the fishing excesses which the report says presently exists within the five companies which are to become two companies. In fact, Mr. Speaker, it is a Bill which suggests that the provincial and federal Governments are nationalizing the fisheries. Yet the federal Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) and the Nova Scotia Minister of Fisheries talk about the privatization of the two companies. How will this take place? What will the Bank of Nova Scotia receive in real terms out of this? Will it be a benefit? What about the company owners, are they receiving a benefit?
We are told in Clause 4 on page 2 of the agreement between the federal Government and Nova Scotia that:
The governments agree that their participation in refinancing the company will be on terms such that the existing shareholders and financial institutions shall not be bailed out.
Yet we see an article in the Daily News in Newfoundland on November 11 stating that the CDC will receive $14.6 million for its shares. Then take that together with an article in the Evening Telegram of November 12 which says the federal Government will pay $14.6 million to the CDC, a major shareholder in Fishery Products.
We have been told shareholders will not benefit in this restructuring. 1 think that question has to be answered in committee because we already see some shareholders getting benefits. I think the people on the East Coast would like to know the answer to this question. Will the Nickersons receive a benefit? On the other hand, we hear they are going into receivership. These are all questions which have to be answered because they concern my constituents and other East Coast Canadians. They should be answered before we proceed further with the restructuring of the Atlantic fishery.
There are other questions about the agreement, Mr. Speaker. Why would the Province of Nova Scotia agree that the Nickerson scallop fleet go to Newfoundland? I would like to know in what way that benefits Newfoundland. I have already spoken about the economic benefits to existing shareholders and financial institutions. 1 am curious to know if we are going to be funding them. Clause 11 on page 3 of the agreement between the federal Government and the Province of Nova Scotia says:
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
The two governments will ask financial institutions to provide credit support to ensure the province's independent fish processors are able to maintain continued normal operations.
I know of several operations in my own area which are suffering because the banks have already increased interest rates as well as dropped the level of financing that the small producers were used to. When will the Province of Nova Scotia go after these institutions? When is the federal Minister going to go after them? How much power do these two Governments have over the financial institutions? Mr. Kirby is quoted in The Globe and Mail of November 5, 1983 as saying:
Governments and the bank have simply become the buyers of last resort, a possibility we had foreseen from the beginning-
1 do not see that in the recommendations.
-if no private investors could be found. And once we decided not to bail anyone out, we knew we were going to have to get something for our money and that something was equity in the new company.
1 know some Members have already asked this question, but what chance were private investors given to invest? Until the company goes into receivership, who can invest?
There are other questions the Bill does not answer. How are these companies to be formed? We are told they will be privately run with provincial and federal money. Who has control over the directors? The bank and the federal Government will appoint directors to each new company in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. Will these directors not have conflicts of interest? It is inconceivable to me that the Bank of Nova Scotia, which will make appointments to both companies, could not make a decision concerning one company which would not be beneficial to the other company. Will there be a conflict of interest concerning the federal Government? What will be the objects of these two companies? Will they operate as a public company in competition with the smaller, independent processors? Or will they operate as a private company? If private, will they be allowed to operate on the basis of good business practices, which might mean the shutting down of some operations as recommended by Dr. Kirby?
The one thing we have is a Bill which gives wide powers, but we have only one arrangement or agreement before us, Mr. Speaker, the one between Newfoundland and the federal Government. We in Nova Scotia are waiting to see what the arrangements will be. There are different players. We do not know what the shareholders in National Sea will do, whether they will accept this agreement to co-operate. We have to wait and see. But in all the recommendations Mr. Kirby and his task force made, I cannot say it was clearly and specifically set out that this is what we would end up with.
There were other things in the Kirby task force report which have not been dealt with. A key example of that is one whole chapter dealing with the herring seining fleet where he recommends there be a Government buy-back to reduce the capacity of that fleet. What is in it for the poor fishermen who are trying to make a living with too few fish and fleet overcapacity? They are being asked to do their own buy-back.
It seems to me that the players who were there prior to Dr. Kirby have not been heard from. That in itself shows a

November 17, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act vacuum and 1 would like to know why. Why are the processors being bailed out, because we hear the CDC is being bailed out? Who else is going to be bailed out? What is going to happen to the other recommendations? Will the seiners be helped? What about all those small fishermen who, over the last few years, have seen their interest rates go up? Are they going to be helped out?
Mr. Speaker, I realize my time is up. It is my hope that the concerns 1 have raised will be fully discussed in committee. Unless we have a clear indication of where this Bill will take us and who it will help and affect, and unless those concerns are answered, we will have many days of graver concern on the East Coast.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-170, the federal Government's legislation to restructure the Atlantic fishery. At the outset, I should make it clear that I have deep-seated reservations about the Bill, especially from the point of view of my own Province of Prince Edward Island.
Prince Edward Island's interests have been all but ignored by the Government, so preoccupied has it been with other East Coast Provinces, notably Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. Yet the Prince Edward Island fishery is an important part of the total industry in Atlantic Canada. Indeed, the fishery is the second largest industry on the Island in terms of jobs and earned income.
The fishery is more than just another industry in the Province. It is an integral part of the culture of the Island. Many communities of the Province, from Tignish to Nufrage, were originally settled because of the fishery. It continues to be the lifeblood of most of those communities to this very day. The fishery is practically the only way of life that the people of that Province have ever known. Salt water is in their veins. To destroy the fishery through Government heavy-handedness, or to allow it to die through neglect or mismanagement, would be to destroy the people themselves.
Therefore, we are debating today not just another piece of legislation, nor simply a plan to rescue yet another industry, though clearly it has elements of that. In fact, we are discussing the survival of an important part of Canada. If such sounds like so much rhetorical hyperbole or flourish, let me assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I am not exaggerating. The Atlantic fishery provides some 100,000 people with jobs, with about equal numbers engaged in the catch and processing sector. That total number is approximately 25,000 more than the members employed in the entire automobile manufacturing industry of this country.
Now, after decades of abject neglect by the federal Government, it has taken a veritable crisis in the fishery to shock the Government into paying any attention at all to this important part of our national life, and only in the form of an after the fact rescue operation rather than in the form of a rational, well thought out, well planned strategy. With most of the large fish plants bankrupt, in receivership or on the verge of it, with thousands of plant workers and fishermen idle and with the entire region reeling from the economic impact, the federal Government has decided at last to take some action.
The Bill before us sets out to do several things. In general, it seeks to provide the legal and financial powers for the federal Government to restructure the Atlantic fishery. The Bill would empower the Government to acquire, hold or dispose of any interest in any enterprise engaged directly or indirectly in the Atlantic fishery. In particular, the Bill provides for an immedi-

November 17, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act ate appropriation of $138 million to finance the federal contribution to the so-called restructuring plan. The bill also authorizes the Government to make loan guarantees to fishery enterprises being restructured. As part of the restructuring, agreements have been signed or tentatively agreed to by the federal Government and Newfoundland and Nova Scotia to restructure the deep sea fishing plants based in those Provinces. In the process, two huge nationalized companies are being forged from the ashes of private companies.
I use the term "nationalized companies" advisedly. The Nova Scotia restructuring agreement will take the two large companies in that Province-National Sea and H. B. Nickerson and Sons-and make one large state-dominated company. The Newfoundland deal takes three major fish firms in the Province-Fishery Products, the Lake group and John Penney and Sons-and creates a massive company controlling 85 per cent of the processing capacity in Newfoundland. The two new super corporations will have the dubious distinction of being, respectively, the largest and second largest fish companies in the entire world.
Let us make no mistake about the matter. The so-called restructuring arrangement is, at once, a full-scale nationalization of the affected parts of the industry and a bail-out of not only the former privately owned companies but also the Bank of Nova Scotia which otherwise would lose millions of dollars in bad loans. Indeed, this scheme is a takeover, not a restructuring at all.
Neither Parliament nor the public has been allowed to know the details of the arrangement. The whole thing has been shrouded in secrecy and mystery from the very beginning. I think one may never find out the whole story. In the case of Nova Scotia, apparently the deal is yet to be finalized. But this much we do know about the Newfoundland deal. I mention it only in the context of my Province of Prince Edward Island which has been, to date, ignored in all of this. The super company is 85 per cent owned by Governments. Eight of the eleven members of the board of directors are Government appointed. The chief executive officer is a joint appointment of both Governments. Significant corporate decisions are subject to the veto of the federal and provincial Governments. Most relevant of all, management must consult both Governments before the company can act. This control is above and beyond that exercised by the federal Government through its general management of the Atlantic fishery.
What the country has received, therefore, is a Government-dominated industry, one in which the state will have a direct day to day vested interest through ownership and control, including corporate voting rights. Decisions affecting the companies, and therefore the industry generally, because of their size and influence, will most certainly be made on the basis of political considerations rather than on the basis of the best interests of the over-all fishery or of the region as a whole. The wonderful people who have made a hash of everything else they have controlled, from Canadair to the post office, are now going to put codfish on our tables.
The restructuring plan has the potential to devastate the fishery in Prince Edward Island, however important or however temporary may be the relief it could provide to Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. It could well ring the death knell to the independently-owned fish processing sector in my Province and consequently to a large part of the rest of the fishery there. The fact is, Sir, there are some 42 fish processing plants in P.E.I. About two dozen of them are independents operating outside the restructured companies and exporting produce on their own. The two largest independents, which process groundfish, are Georgetown Seafoods Ltd. in Georgetown and Usen Fisheries in Souris. The former, Georgetown, has not been in operation since the fall of 1981 but Usen and most of the smaller plants throughout the Province have been fully operational and profitable.
1 do not know what will become of Georgetown Seafoods. P.E.I.'s Minister in the federal cabinet, the Hon. Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell), has been saying from one end of P.E.I. to the other that the plant's reopening is imminent. He was saying that as long ago as last spring and early summer. Yet in reply to my questions in the House as recently as October 7, the federal Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) refused to associate himself with that commitment given by his colleague.
Moreover, a secret federal Government document prepared by the Ministry of State for Economic and Regional Expansion last summer and obtained by the research office of my Party made very clear that the plant, in the eyes of the Government, was "permanently closed". Here we had a secret Government document, at a time when the federal Minister of Veterans Affairs was saying that the reopening of the plant was imminent, making it clear that, in the eyes of the same Government, the Georgetown Seafoods plant was permanently closed and its reopening was not imminent, as the Minister was pointing out.
Obviously, the future is grim for that plant. I believe the best bet is for the plant to reopen under provincial auspices and it is to be hoped with private investment money. But for that to happen, Georgetown Seafoods will need to be given back four of the original 11 trawlers still in the hands of the existing owners, H. B. Nickerson and Sons Limited. Those trawlers are now at Canso, having long since been wrenched from Georgetown, leaving it virtually impossible for the plant to operate profitably.
The new restructuring package has nonetheless loaded the deck of cards against all the independent plants across P.E.I. and, indeed, throughout the Atlantic region and parts of Quebec. Now, the federal Government is to be in the fish processing business itself in a massive way, why should it want to encourage competition against itself? From here on, the Government will hold all the aces. Who but the most extreme optimist would believe that the Government will not weight future programs and regulations in favour of its own client
November 17, 1983

companies, to the detriment of the remaining private
companies?
Even before the restructuring, the federal Government controlled everything from dredging operations to fishing quotas, to federal wharf construction, to DREE-type industry subsidies, to total allowable catches, to fish processing plant health standards, to import licences. Now the small, independent operators also face the prospect of having to compete against huge Government-owned and Government-subsidized fish companies in an industry where the Government could set all the rules to benefit its own industrial giants.
I have been in touch with many of the independent operators in my Province of P.E.I. and with both Premier Jim Lee and Fisheries Minister Roddy Pratt. Most of those operators are petrified about the potential impact of Bill C-170 on their plants. One such operator told me that if Bill C-170 passes as it stands he may as well close shop immediately. I know many others feel the same way. More and more of the independents are joining the Federation of Independent Fish Packers, recently formed for the sole purpose of fighting Bill C-170 that we are debating today. Premier Lee and Mr. Pratt share those concerns and fears, and I do too.
Independent operators have been assured by the federal Minister of Fisheries and Oceans that the restructuring arrangement is only a temporary one, made to support the fishery until it can find its sea legs, so to speak-stand on its own two feet. Assurances have also been given by the Minister and by other spokesmen for the Government that the new Government companies will then be returned to the private sector; they will be privatized. I ask you, Sir, if that is actually to be the case, why is the Government afraid to incorporate such a provision right into the legislation itself? There is absolutely nothing in the existing Bill to protect the independents.
I urge the Government to devise a new section to provide for the Government's orderly withdrawal from an ownership position in the industry according to a detailed schedule. Such a section should either specify a date by which all Government equity must be sold or, alternatively, set a limit on its equity; for example, less than 40 per cent by 1986. A section of that kind would have the effect of making the relevant assistance under the so-called restructuring program a one-shot impetus to the industry, not a prescription for permanent nationalization of it.
Bill C-170 is so important to P.E.I. and to all of Atlantic Canada that it should go immediately, or as soon as everyone has had his or her say, to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry for detailed study. Obviously, the Liberal chairman of that Committee, the Hon. Member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell), who just spoke at some length, shares my deep-seated reservations and concerns about Bill C-170, for she is quoted in La Presse, as I pointed out a few moments ago, on November 16, as saying that "fishermen and small businesses have numerous reasons for concern about the future this restructuring holds for them".

Mr. Speaker, I represent a federal riding in Quebec where, as one of the municipal authorities in the Gaspe said recently on national television, fishing is the only valid alternative to unemployment and welfare. Today, Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to underline the very substantial role played by the federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans in taking this industry in hand, and the Department's very definite intention to provide for restructuring of this industry through Bill C-170.
The House will recall that Quebec's Atlantic coast extends for over more than 3,000 kilometers. Here and there along the cost, there are a number of very small villages that depend largely on fishing, not only for a living but for their very survival.
That, Mr. Speaker, will be the focus of my comments in support of the legislation to restructure the Atlantic fisheries.
Not long ago, the TV news showed us some tragic pictures of Gaspe fishermen who were obliged to throw a day's catch back into the sea, because they were unable to find any fish depots that would take the herring they caught the day before. These fishermen had just been confronted with the dilemma that arises when supply exceeds demand and shore facilities can no longer handle the landing capacity of the fishing fleet. On television the situation even more dramatic, of course, but the point was very clearly made that such occurrences were not unique in the Gaspe.

November 17, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
In its report, the Atlantic Fisheries Task Force had already commented at length on the lack of infrastructures in the fisheries industry in Quebec, as well as on the need for restructuring, without delay, the entire industry in that Province and Eastern Canada, so as to make it economically viable, provide a decent income for Canadians employed in the industry and finally, to serve the interests of all Canadians.
As a result of the recommendations made by the task force in its report, it was clear that it would be necessary to reorganize the management of Quebec's ocean fisheries and also to renovate and modernize existing infrastructures in order to meet the pressing needs of an industry which in Quebec, in any case, had a lot of catching up to do.
it is also true, however, that in Quebec, there was a situation where responsibility for ocean fisheries was either shared or duplicated, and as a result, both levels of government were able to blame each other and meanwhile, for instance, equipment that came under one jurisdiction rather than another was allowed to deteriorate through lack of maintenance. In any case, this industry, which is not a major one for the Province but is very important to the Gaspe and especially to the riding of Gaspe, is desperately in need of upgrading, which will require very substantial funding by the level of government that will be taking on this responsibility.
I realize that the fisheries industry in Eastern Canada has experienced very severe problems in recent years. In the Atlantic provinces, there have been times when business was very poor and the threat of bankruptcy continues to hover over the fisheries. After long and stormy negotiations, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) managed to obtain a consensus on restructuring the fisheries industry in such a way that both the provinces and the private sector would share the cost and together make the effort required to revive the industry.
The Minister is therefore to be congratulated on the success of this manoeuvre, thanks to which this time, at least, the Government of Canada will not be left to bear the financial burden and related responsibilities alone.
Unfortunately, the Government of Quebec is still dragging its feet and would rather fund other projects instead of contributing towards the restructuring of this new industry over which it claims exclusive jurisdiction. This would in fact create a kind of enclave in a system where all parties are closely dependent on one another.
After concluding agreements with the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador and the Government of Nova Scotia, and after clearly indicating his intentions to the Government of Quebec, the Minister is asking the House today to give him the means to fully implement a plan that has had a very positive start. In his speech in support of Bill C-170 which is now before the House, the Minister amply demonstrated how complex the issue is and how directly it depends on the
proposed restructuring. He made it very clear that he was anxious to give all partners in this plan an opportunity to be heard and to express their points of view. He emphasized they should be given an opportunity to contribute directly to and, eventually, to benefit, both individually and collectively from, the results of this plan.
Last week, when I visited my riding, 1 met several hundred fishermen and processing plant workers. They were very concerned about the future of the fisheries industry in Quebec, as a result of what the Minister responsible for fisheries in Quebec, the Hon. Jean Garon, was doing in the Gaspe. Since he became Minister of Fisheries, Mr. Garon's actions have been based far more on his political views than on any concern for the social and economic welfare of producers and fishermen in the riding of Gaspe and the Province of Quebec.
My constituents have asked me to inform the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans that he should proceed with his plan for restructuring the fisheries industry, because in the past, it was always the Government of Canada that managed to save the fishermen of the Province of Quebec.
Between 1975 and 1978, a decision was made to revive the groundfish industry in Eastern Canada. During that time, the Government of Canada gave Quebec fishermen and producers grants amounting to $6,111,400. In 1976 and 1977, Quebec fishing enterprises received subsidies totalling $566,000 for ships of 100 feet or more, based in the Gulf, so that they could go outside the Gulf to fish and unload inside the Gulf. In 1972, Mr. Speaker ... I believe I may call it one o'clock?

-the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans introduced a program to protect Atlantic salmon and to stop commercial fishing, starting that year. The Government of Canada paid Atlantic and Gulf fishermen, including the Gaspe, to put away their fishing gear and refrain from fishing salmon commercially since 1972. In the Gaspe, people remember this, and they realize that it has always been the Government of Canada that managed to save fishermen in the province of Quebec. Mr. Speaker, may 1 call it one o'clock?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are worried by statements of the Governments of the United States, El Salvador, Honduras, Guatamela and Costa Rica, threatening military invasion of Nicaragua and of the liberated areas of El Salvador. Although Nicaragua and the El Salvador guerrillas have each repeatedly offered to negotiate, the U.S. and those Governments it dominates have refused any answer except to build up huge armies and navies for invasion.
The Canadian Government, after being shamefully deceived by the U.S. Government about its intention to invade and occupy Grenada, cannot trust the U.S. Government to give honest information about its intentions against the peoples of Nicaragua and El Salvador. Therefore, 1 call on the Canadian Government to establish our independent presence in Nicaragua by sending our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) to Nicaragua to discuss their recent proposals for mutual disarmament and removal of foreign military personnel, with on-site inspection, by opening an embassy in Managua to provide direct, independent day-today information about the illegal attacks by U.S. backed Somocistas, and by working closely with the Contadora group to block U.S. plans for war and to increase economic aid to Nicaragua.

Mr. Speaker, two days ago the northern portion of the island state of Cyprus seceded from that country and proclaimed itself an independent state. To sensitive, fair-minded people everywhere this is an unnecessary, tragic development in the life of the Cypriot people. As a Canadian living in a bilingual state and a multicultural society, I firmly reject the premise motivating the coup-that Greek and Turkish Cypriots are so fundamentally different in their lifestyles and aspirations that previous attempts to work out an accommodation within the established internationally recognized borders of the state should now be abandoned.
No one should forget that Greek and Turkish Cypriots had lived together in peace and prosperity for a generation before the armed might of the Turkish forces viciously divided the island. That experience must mean something. Surely it proves that the two cultures can co-exist, even thrive, under a common Cypriot citizenship.
Diversity is rapidly becoming one of the dominant features of the modern world. A wise leader knows that, and tries to build bridges, not walls. Mr. Rauf Danktash's actions have betrayed the history of the people of Cyprus and subverted the bright promise of their future. He should be roundly condemned by all of us in this House.

ADMISSION OF AFGHAN REFUGEES TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask why the Government of Canada treats the estimated 4.5 million Afghan refugees who are now in Pakistan and Iran in a different manner than it treats refugees from Poland, Central America and elsewhere? One of my constituents recently returned from visiting his family in the camps in Pakistan and said that the impression there is that the Canadian Government sides with the Soviet Union on its invasion of Afghanistan.
I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that since 1979 Canada has accepted a total of only about 200 refugees from Afghanistan. West Germany and the United States have each accepted several thousand. Why can we in Canada not declare the Afghan refugees as a designated class for the upcoming year? I also remind you, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian aid to the Afghan refugees is currently running at about $6 per refugee per year.
In the words of Professor M. S. Noorzoy of the Afghan Cultural and Charitable Society of Alberta, Afghan refugees "come with skills and education, but above all, with a great desire to re-establish themselves productively without delay". Canadians generally believe that human beings everywhere should be treated with dignity and respect.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs who is used to being between a rock and a hard place. My question concerns the Bank of Nova Scotia which is being fined $25,000 a day by U.S. courts for not divulging bank records from the Grand Cayman Islands. Would the Minister advise the House whether the Government has made a decision to intervene before the U.S. courts to aid the Bank of Nova Scotia?
