speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: GRAND CAYMAN ISLANDS-LEGAL STATUS OF BANK OF NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the meeting with Mr. Schultz, the answer is yes. We did have a continuing consultation on what Canada considers an unjustified extraterritorial application of American law. In this case the Bank of Nova Scotia and other banks are put in an almost impossible position in being asked to comply with American law which contravenes the local law. The American authorities have sought information in a way which we think is unnecessary as well as unjustified. We believe that a good deal of that information could be obtained legally through the application, for example, for the taxation treaties. All of this was discussed with Mr. Schultz. We have attempted to put in place some mechanism that will overcome this difficulty.
The Hon. Member asked whether we intend to intervene in support of the Bank of Nova Scotia before the American court. That matter is under consideration by the Department of Justice. I believe there is an intention to file an amicus brief or take that status at court. As far as I know, the exact details of the statement are still under consideration by the Department of Justice.

subsubtopic: MR. BLENKARN-SUGGESTED IRREGULARITY IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (B)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order. 1 want to draw to your attention a vote in Supplementary Estimates (B) that I feel is out of order. It is Vote 6b under Consumer and Corporate Affairs. It deals with the payment to the Canada Post Corporation for special purposes of $8,109,406. The Estimates outline "special purposes" as being the relocation of the philatelic mail order service to Antigonish, Nova Scotia; special employment initiatives; a grant of some kind for propane vehicle conversion; special construction repair projects and federal off-oil conversion.
Over the years, Mr. Speaker, you and your predecessors have ruled that the appropriations process should not be used as a substitute for legislation. To quote Madam Speaker's ruling of June 12, 1981:
-the government may not by the use of an Appropriation Act obtain authority that it does not have under existing legislation.
There is no legislative authority in the Canada Post Corporation Act to do the kind of things set out in this estimate. I would like to read into the record Section 28 of the Canada Post Corporation Act. Perhaps it is not necessary to read it in full but let me read Subsections (1), (2) and (3):
28. (1) Where at any time the available revenues of the Corporation are not sufficient to pay all the operating and income charges of the Corporation as and when due, the Minister of Finance, on the application of the Corporation approved by the Minister, may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, place at the disposal of the Corporation such amounts as may be required to enable the Corporation to meet all such charges.
(2)	All amounts placed at the disposal of the Corporation pursuant to subsection (1) shall be reimbursed to the Minister of Finance from the annual revenues of the Corporation in so far as such revenues are sufficient.
(3)	Where the annual revenues of the Corporation are insufficient for the purposes of subsection (2), the Minister shall cause the amount of the insufficiency to be included, in the form of a deficit appropriation item, in the next Appropriation Act laid before Parliament thereafter.
Nowhere in the Act is there any authority for an appropriation that is not an appropriation to pay losses. This is not a question of losses. This is a question of the post office entering into a series of activities that have nothing to do with its losses. Clearly if there were a loss in the post office, an appropriation could be made for the loss in accordance with Section 28 of the Act. But there is no provision in the Canada Post Corporation
November 17, 1983

Act for an appropriation to move an activity of the post office to Antigonish Nova Scotia. There is no provision for a loss, for special employment initiatives. It is not a loss necessarily to conduct a federal propane vehicle conversion program. In effect, what is happening is that this estimate is totally out of order.
I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to investigate the matter. If 1 am right, and I believe I am, that Section 28 of the Canada Post Corporation Act does not allow this kind of estimate, 1 ask that the estimate be disallowed and removed from the proposed appropriation Bill.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. De Bane that Bill C-170, an Act to authorize investment in and the provision of financial assistance to the Atlantic Fisheries for the purpose of restructuring certain fishery enterprises, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.

Mr. Speaker, before recess, I was talking about the various times since 1970 that the Government of Canada has intervened to help fishermen in the Province of Quebec. 1 said that under its program to re-establish the Canadian groundfish industry, the Government of Canada had paid Quebec fishermen and processors grants totalling $6,684,400 between 1975 and 1978.
Furthermore, that in 1972, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans introduced a program to protect Atlantic salmon. He had to suspend commercial salmon fishing in the Gulf, and again. The Government of Canada subsidized ninety-five salmon fishermen, from 1972 to 1980, spending a total of $1,840,000 or an average of about $20,000 for every salmon fisherman in the Province of Quebec.
In the summer of 1982, there was utter chaos in the fisheries industry as a result of the dire situation at Pecheurs-Unis. Here again, the Government of Canada stepped in to save the fishermen. In the spring of 1983, there was a recurrence of the same problem at Pecheurs-Unis, and the Government of Canada guaranteed a bank loan so that Pecheurs-Unis could start its operations and fishermen could start their fishing season.
Mr. Speaker, we, the people of the Gaspe, are not blind. We know what the Government of Canada has done for the fisheries industry in Quebec.
Within the framework of the Economic Development Plan for the Gaspe and Lower St. Lawrence, a total of $29,500,000 will be spent on the fisheries industry in the Gaspe in the next two years, for the construction of facilities for handling and
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act unloading fish, manufacturing and storing ice, storing and distributing bait, and also for improving harbour facilities in the area. These funds are being contributed exclusively by the Government of Canada.
What has the PQ Government done since it came to power for fishermen in the Gaspe, the Magdalen Islands and on the North Shore?
Looking back, Mr. Speaker, we see that first of all, this Government did away with gillnet subsidies; second, it cut in half the Quebec Government's subsidy on insurance premiums for fishing boats; third, it abolished the subsidy program for lobster trap replacement; fourth, it closed several ice depots; fifth, it raised the price of ice provided by departmental depots from $8 to $20 per ton; and finally, it introduced its special tax on gas which put a heavy burden on fishermen and fish processors.
I could go on for much longer, Mr. Speaker, but that is how the Hon. Jean Garon has helped Quebec's fishermen.
During the week's holiday we spent in our ridings, 1 also met independent processors from the Gaspe. They realize that restructuring of the fisheries industry is necessary. Through their ability, initiative and sheer hard work, these processors have helped to maintain fisheries-related operations in the Gaspe and Quebec.
Private entreprise is absolutely essential to the future of the fisheries industry in Quebec and the Atlantic Provinces. The independent processors are also concerned about what will happen to their processing plants when a new giant company is established, with the majority of shares being held by the Government of Canada. They are not necessarily opposed to this new fisheries corporation based in the Gaspe, but they would urge the Government to set up management and control mechanisms in order to protect private enterprise.
We must not make it difficult for private enterprise to develop, to progress and to create jobs. If private enterprise were to disappear from the fisheries industry in Quebec and the Atlantic Provinces, the resulting economic disaster would be far worse than the bankruptcy of Pecheurs-Unis. In the past, members of local co-operatives have had many problems with Pecheurs-Unis du Quebec. Today they are very pleased this organization will disappear when the new corporation is established, once the legislation before the House today. Bill C-170, is passed.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, 1 urge Hon. Members to join me in supporting this Bill to restructure the Atlantic fisheries and to provide for financial assistance by the Government of Canada in defraying the cost of this restructuring, because of all the Canadians who depend on this and, perhaps also, because every day, our fishermen are exploring the living resources of our ocean boundaries and it is up to us to take advantage of these resources.

November 17, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
In committee, we shall be able to suggest amendments to this Bill. This morning, my colleague from South West Nova (Miss Campbell) wanted the Vice-Chairman, the Member for Gaspe, to chair the committee while this Bill is being considered. 1 can assure my hon. colleague that we can share the duties of conducting the debate in committee and thus ensure that the legislation is passed by the House before this session is adjourned.

speechtext: Are there Hon. Members rising to ask questions of the Hon. Member who has just spoken? If not, the Chair will recognize the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis).

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise today to speak to Bill C-170, an Act to authorize the investment in and the provision of financial assistance to the Atlantic fisheries for the purpose of restructuring certain fisheries enterprises. I do recognize that this is perhaps the most important fisheries debate of any that we have had in this session of Parliament. I believe it was the Premier of Newfoundland who indicated that this was perhaps the most important phenomenon to happen to the Island of Newfoundland and Labrador since Confederation. I find it disheartening, though, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane), who sponsored this Bill, does not see fit to be in the House. While one might be able to understand the Minister's absence, I find it difficult to understand that even the Parliamentary Secretary is unable to be in attendance in the House of Commons today.
It is an insult. Shame!

It really is an insult, Mr. Speaker, to the Atlantic fisheries and to fishermen and fish processors across this country. I think it indicates pretty clearly just how seriously Members of the Government take this particular legislation. I appreciate that what this Bill really represents to Canada, Mr. Speaker, is a recognition of what happens when there is a lack of adequate planning, a lack of any comprehensive planning regarding one of Canada's major economic sectors. Obviously, we are seeing today the result of what happens when the federal Government does not sit down with provincial Governments and with representatives of the fishing industry in order to develop some long-range comprehensive planning strategies. The result is that we have today what amounts, by and large, to a bail-out situation, throwing a lifesaver to an industry which has been extremely hard-pressed over the last number of months.
I would like to say that this particular drastic measure which we are looking at today is the result of Government activities, in part, over the last number of years, and the incredible optimism which both the provincial and federal Governments brought about in the industry because of the expansion of the 200-mile limit, with the suggestion that this was a sector of the economy, the Atlantic fisheries sector,
which virtually had unlimited opportunities and potential. People were encouraged to move into areas in which they were previously hesitant to move. Corporations, both large and small, were encouraged to borrow beyond their means in anticipation of this incredible bubble which was about to occur in terms of the Atlantic fisheries. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that management decisions resulted in a great deal of over-capitalization and unnecessary debt which precipitated and persuaded the Government to act in this very dramatic way.
We also, of course, recognize that the present problems were compounded by the monetarist position which the federal Government took a number of years ago. I might say it was a position which was supported by the Conservative Party of Canada, represented through its short term in office by the then Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister, who supported the position of Governor Bouey and the Bank of Canada. This position was later taken up by the present Government. It was essentially a Government policy of high interest rates, Mr. Speaker, the recognition that high interest rates would somehow cause investors to hesitate to make the necessary investments, which would cause the economy to wind down, slow down, and that is exactly what happened. We are looking at a situation, Mr. Speaker, in the Atlantic fishery, where, because of this high interest rate policy of the present Government and of the short-lived Conservative Government, fishermen, fish producers and fish processors were simply unable to operate effectively and efficiently. I will also say, Mr. Speaker, that these problems were compounded by the rather political nature of the DREE program, by the sort of indiscriminate throwing of DREE money out for political gain; some DREE money here, some DREE grants there. This resulted in a fisheries infrastructure unfolding which was not always based on economic advice and common sense.
Similarly, there was the indiscriminate doling out of licences, which resulted in there being more fishermen than the industry could support. As a result of that, restrictive regulations were brought in by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, which compounded the problem. I believe the most obvious over-exuberant expectations of what the 200-mile limit would bring about were demonstrated when the Department decided to dole out international fishing licences to foreigners to fish in our waters. That again was simply another factor which contributed to depleted resources and more pressure being brought to bear on an already over-extended resource.
This major problem of an industry which has floundered for years and years as a result of a lack of Government strategy in place can be seen on the West Coast of this country. Again, as a result of a lack of any real strategic planning with all the players involved, and with the lack of a comprehensive strategy for that resource sector, an ad hoc approach has been taken, which has resulted in chaos on both the East and West Coasts of Canada. It was certainly known many, many years ago that this would be bound to unfold in this way.
I remember the economic development task force, which was conducted by the New Democratic Party in Atlantic
November 17, 1983

Canada. Various fishermen's organizations and various fishing organizations brought to our attention at that time the financial and economic plight of the industry. However, the action the Government took was to appoint the Kirby task force, which of course resulted in Bill C-170 which we are debating today, the restructuring of the fishing industry into two fishing giants.
While having two giants in that industry will place it amongst the largest fishing corporations in the world, it raises a number of concerns. One of the major concerns 1 have is what this Bill provides in terms of power to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. The Minister may acquire shares, debentures or securities of any fishery enterprise. The Minister may make a contribution or loan to any fishery enterprise. I use those two references in the Bill to show the unlimited powers which the Minister will receive if this Bill passes. Mr. Speaker, 1 feel that that ought to raise concern among Canadians generally because we are really being asked, as Members of Parliament, to have faith in the good intentions of the Minister. Through us he is asking people in the fishing industry of Atlantic Canada to have faith in what this Minister plans to do for the industry. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, when one looks at the rather abysmal record of the Government and the Minister regarding this very critical fisheries sector, I do not believe it is a reasonable request for the Minister to make.
As the critic for fisheries in our Party has indicated, this Bill really does not solve the problem. It simply breathes life into an ailing industry. What happens from this point on will be really critical. This is simply the first of a long trek to revitalize and restructure that very ailing industry.
I believe it is important to note the role of the banks in this solution. We have not to this point recognized that one of the reasons that the Government moved as it did to restructure financially this ailing industry was to provide relief to the banks which were involved. It was well known that virtually every chartered bank in this country was heavily in debt as a result of imprudent loans made to a number of large and small corporations. Once again, as we have seen so often in the past, Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada, the taxpayers of Canada, through the Government of Canada, have been asked to come in and bail out a number of corporations. And 1 believe that really the motivation has been to bail out the banks which found themselves over-extended in this very critical industry.
We have made a great deal of effort in Bill C-170 to assist some of the large players in the Atlantic fishery, including the Bank of Nova Scotia. But what about the 700 independents who have been left out of the equation and are now looking with some fear at these two megagiants in the fishing industry? They are being asked to compete alongside these major players. Are the banks going to be sympathetic to their plight? Absolutely not, Mr. Speaker. We have already seen the major chartered banks of this country saying to the fishermen that they are cutting back the lines of credit, they no longer have faith in the industry or the fishermen and their traditional
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act lines of credit are being reduced virtually as a matter of bank policy. When you consider the privileged position of banks in this country, Mr. Speaker, when you consider the responsibility they ought to accept as a result of that privileged position, this is not the kind of behaviour we would expect from our major lending institutions.
I believe it is critical that the Government of Canada view this problem not simply in cold, hard financial terms. There is the impression that the Government plans to privatize this restructured corporate amalgamation. While one will perhaps laud that as a long-term goal, 1 do hope we do not lose sight of the fact that, in getting these restructured companies back on their feet financially and then selling them off to the private sector, there is more to it than that.
I believe that what we are seeing here is not only a financial and economic problem, it is also a social problem. Because of the dependence of so many medium and small communities in Atlantic Canada on the fishing industry, an ailing industry will result in a tearing of the social fabric in many of those communities. After all, for a great deal of Atlantic Canada fishing is Atlantic Canada. What happens to the fishing industry, not only these restructured companies but the small independents as well, will reflect on the social fabric of Atlantic Canada in the months, years and decades ahead.
I urge, Mr. Speaker, that the Government keep in mind that financial viability is a major factor but it is not the only factor, and I suspect we can make a case that it is not the major factor. Long-term employment of people in Atlantic Canada, long-term economic stability in the fishing industry, ought to be the number one priority, as opposed to a rapid move to financial viability and a turnover to the private sector of these new-found corporations.
I want to take issue with some comments made by certain Members of the House, Mr. Speaker. The concern was expressed that the provincial and federal Governments, as well as the fishing companies, did not look actively enough for foreign money to come to the rescue. I think it is time that we as Canadians stood up and stopped using taxpayers' money to bribe foreign corporations into coming into this country. 1 believe, as do Members of the New Democratic Party, that we can do it ourselves. There is money in this country to do it ourselves. We do not have to go out on bended knee with grants and give-aways to the Japanese, Americans, Germans or others. We can do it ourselves.
I shudder at the number of people who have suggested in debate on this bill that we should have gone to foreign investors in foreign countries for the answer to our fisheries problem. If one could be so bold, one could perhaps argue the case that one of the reasons we have problems in many of our resource industries today is that in the past that is exactly what we did. We went outside of this country and asked foreigners to come in and make the investments, and more important the investment decisions, for this industry and the future of Canadians. I hope the days are long past when we have to look to foreigners to make a decision regarding the Canadian economy. I repeat, we do not need to use taxpayers'

November 17, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
money to bribe foreign corporations to assist us in the bail-out of this particular industry.
I want to close, Mr. Speaker, by suggesting that this provides an ideal opportunity for the Government to show some real leadership in carrying out its intention to divest itself of these investments in due time. The Government should consider other viable alternatives simply to privatizing this organization. 1 raise as a concern the possibility of major co-operatives becoming involved. In other words, the fish producers and processors, the fishermen themselves in Atlantic Canada, are quite capable of running many of these corporations. They are quite capable of making the necessary management decisions. 1 think it is time we gave people credit where credit is due. These individuals have spent every working day of their lives in the fishing industry in one form or another, and to suggest they are somehow unable to make the necessary management decisions is a slight to these individuals. I believe the Government now has the opportunity, as it moves out of its involvement in the months and years ahead, to look at the people involved in these corporations to play a more meaningful role than they have often played in the past, particularly when it comes to making financial decisions of a marketing or investment nature.
While we in the NDP will do everything possible to remove any impediment to a rapid passage of this Bill, we do want to use the opportunity of second reading, when we are asked to comment on the principle of the Bill, to make it clear that one of the reasons we are in this situation today is the lack of attention paid to planning the future of this industry, particularly given the Government's monetarist policy concerning high interest rates. Rather than see this as a time of gloom and doom, as some other Members have suggested, we see it as a time of opportunity to place in the hands of those people in Atlantic Canada who are directly involved the opportunity to participate in the development of the Atlantic fishery to the maximum extent possible.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am glad to have an opportunity to speak on Bill C-170, the Atlantic fisheries restructuring Bill. I speak as a very concerned Nova Scotian rather than as a Member who at the present time has a very large fishing constituency. I used to have, and my colleague across the way from Central Nova inherited, that part of Digby which was one of the real king counties for fish in Nova Scotia. My heritage lies in Digby county and I can thereby relate very much to the concern in that county, and frankly in all of Nova Scotia, about the implications of this Bill. This is part of the paradox. It is the very size of the industry in Atlantic Canada, which employs about 100,000 people compared to the 75,000 employed in the auto industry, which we hear so much about from time to time in Ontario. Considering that there are 100,000 people in Atlantic Canada involved directly and indirectly in the fishing industry, one should appreciate the concern over this Bill. In effect, that compounds the problem because we know the industry is in "dire straits", to quote a famous phrase. It is in dire straits because of the mismanagement of the industry,
because of Government policy, Government action and Government inaction.
When our fishing spokesman, the Member from South Shore (Mr. Crouse), replied to the Minister here on Monday he outlined, as other Members have, all the problems that the fishing industry had with a lot of the political interference that has adversely affected the fishing industry in terms of licenses, quotas and seasons. The entrepreneurial industry and the skills of those who ply the seas have really been hamstrung by Government interference and Government policy.
In the brief time that I have 1 am not going to review all those details. They were most ably reviewed by the Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse). We also had a very interesting speech this morning from the Member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell). She is the Chairman of the Fisheries and Forestry Committee and has real concerns about this Bill. I am not going to waste the time of the House recounting what this Bill does. We know that the Government is pumping many millions of dollars into the industry to help it, but also thereby bailing out the banks who have over-extended credit to several of the major companies, two in Nova Scotia and three in Newfoundland. Out of this infusion of capital there are going to be two large fishing corporations, the largest and the second largest fishing companies in the world.
Mr. Speaker, we can bandy words about. I do not know what the official name is going to be for this new corporation or new corporations. I am apprehensive after having seen what happened with PetroCan and its establishment. It was the window in the industry, and there are some positive things to say about it. There are also things to be said about PetroCan and the national energy policy whereby PetroCan gets an unfair advantage against competitors in the oil and gas field. The new corporation, which I will call FishCan, for lack of a better word, may also have preferential treatment through the back door from a Government that is giving the funds. It is only natural to say that if the Government is going to create this Crown corporation, when the bottom lines are faced in the administration of a new corporation, the fears of the independent fish operators in Nova Scotia have a lot of merit. Until the lines of administration of the new corporation are defined and queried in the Committee I think those concerns are going to stay.
1 listened to the comments of the Member from the New Democratic Party who preceded me about some of his hopes and some of the ideology of the New Democratic Party. I cannot understand how we can have blind faith that the Government, which created the problem through this new corporation, is now going to be able to cure it. I can quote the political phrase of a former Minister of Finance who said those immortal words, "short-term pain for long-term gain". I am seriously concerned that because we see the carrot of many millions of dollars to help an immediate problem we are going to have short-term gain for long-term pain in the fishing
November 17, 1983

industry until we define how this new corporation is going to operate.
Mr. Speaker, the politicians across the way, and on this side too, have said with authority that the new corporation is not a Crown corporation in the sense of a Crown corporation. In actual fact, it is not. It is worse. It is strictly a creature of the federal Government with no one on the board from the private sector in Newfoundland. If we take that as a precedent for what might happen in Nova Scotia, we are getting a situation in terms of an administration of a corporation doing business which has to be approved by both levels of the Government, by the board and by political appointees. The problem is going to be compounded and not resolved. Regardless of how you lay down the rules, the Government is going to become a more dominant player than it already is. The Government already has a dominant interest in the fishing industry through its licensing practice, quotas and all the inspections it does. With all that dominance before the creation of the corporation, I do not have faith that the new corporation is going to be the cure that we are all hoping for in this very important industry.
I sympathize with those Members who have fishing communities in their constituencies where the plants are closed down and the boats are not at sea because the prices are down. If there were a free vote, which there is not going to be, it would be very difficult for them to vote against the Bill because of some of the principles that I think are wrong in this Bill. Philosophically, I have real difficulty, in terms of the history of Parliament, with the creation of Crown corporations to do business, not Crown corporations to do cultural things such as the CBC. The CNR was born out of a morass of bankruptcies in the railways and was a needed and necessary social creation. In some ways I can understand the argument for the social need for the Crown corporation.
Using the analogy of driving a car which goes off the highway and you need some help, you are obviously going to take help from anyone who comes along to give you help. However, you are not going to take help with as much confidence if the person who forces you off the road is the person who offers you the helping hand. I think that is the case here. I do not know if this new Crown corporation is going to be the octopus of the industry which will reach out with tentacles and unfairly choke, in a discriminatory way the independent fish operations. I do not know if it is going to be the shark of the industry which will eat some of the independent fish operators. 1 do not know if it is going to be a nice little sunfish which will sit in the sea with the other independent operators and get along with everybody in harmony.
Mr. Speaker, when the choice has to be made between the Crown corporation and the independent fish operator, it is only human and natural to say that the Government Crown corporation, which I call FishCan, is going to cut the deck for FishCan and not for the independent operator.
Mr. Speaker, there are so many questions that one has to ask. We all live by the sea in Atlantic Canada. It is part of our pulse. The sea is the womb of the earth. You cannot get away from that beat of the sea. I am proud of it. May I interject
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
now to say that I am glad that my colleague, the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), stood down to let me speak now so that I could catch a plane. He will be speaking later in his most eloquent style.
The sea is fundamental to us. I am appalled as a Canadian that this bounty of the sea is there to feed Canadians and the world. I would like to have the hopes of my friend from the Okanagan who spoke a little while ago. The reality is that we have mucked it up. We need to have questions answered. We have to know about the potential political power of FishCan against the independent operators. We have to know if there is going to be a back door subsidization program greater than what is there now in the infusion of initial funding. We have to know what the reality is about the privatization and the recognition. Is this just a temporary measure to help out an industry that is in dire straits for a time, or is it really going to be there forever and a day?
We used to look around the city of Ottawa and see temporary wartime Government buildings. They stayed there for 45 years. The most temporary law, which is still very much a part of the system of Canada, was the temporary Income Tax Act of 1917. That was a temporary measure. I suggest that we are dreaming in technicolour if we think that this is a temporary measure and the FishCan Corporation will back off once the immediate job is, hopefully, completed and the sales return, the prices rise and people get back to work. I believe we will be moving an amendment which will force Members to show if they believe that it really will back off in a programmed manner as the industry improves. It will be a sunset clause and we will see what happens when the Minister appears before the committee.
I do not get upset over socialization or nationalization. I fully support some of our Crown corporations such as Canadian National, Air Canada and the CBC. These have been creatures of compromise, talent and necessity which, despite the problems they do have, have done well and have provided a social need. That does not bother me. This is the creation of a state corporation but it is being called restructuring, according to the new jargon. I suggest it is misleading, especially for Members opposite who avoid mentioning socialization or nationalization and keep talking about restructuring. A rose is a rose by any name and a rose has thorns as well as a bloom.
I am suggesting most seriously to the House that in reality this is not a restructuring but a back door nationalization of the fish industry.
The Minister will have to be prepared to tell the committee what Canada's position will be with our friends to the south where the great fish market is. What will be the American reaction to public money going into this new FishCan Corporation when the U.S. is already apprehensive about many of our raw resources? They are already attacking the import of our potatoes and other raw resources into the States with countervailing duties, and if they believe there is an unfair advantage from using taxpayers' money to compete against

November 17, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
their private interest, what assurance can the Minister give that the Americans will not slap on countervailing duties when we create the FishCan Corporation here? Because we can be sure that fish lobby in the New England States will say it is unfair trade. There are many questions which the Minister must answer before I will say how I will vote on this legislation at third reading.
The question is, what are the alternatives? They are difficult and, fortunately for Nova Scotia, we are still negotiating. There is not an agreement yet, as there is in Newfoundland. We have not received the assurances as yet from the federal Government, which 1 presume satisfied Newfoundland. I can think of several compromises in Nova Scotia, one of which would be one company going down and the other running the fleet. I personally believe that the record of Governments coming in after the event, having created the problem, is not good. We must face the reality. While it could happen that companies will fail and the fish stocks and inventories will deflate the market even further, that is the reality. Perhaps we should face that situation rather than postpone it for another two years while building up the infrastructure with the bureaucracy that is necessary to run a FishCan operation.
As I said earlier, 1 have real concerns about this temporary measure. We will see how serious Members are about its being temporary when the Member for South Shore perhaps moves his sunset provision. 1 suggest to my friend for South West Nova (Miss Campbell) that the Income Tax Act in 1917 was a temporary measure, and yet. 1 am not very confident about a return to private industry when I read the words of the Machiavellian author who is perhaps behind the whole thing. He is our friend, Dr. Kirby from Nova Scotia. He is an interesting individual with whom 1 have stimulating conversations on planes back and forth to Ottawa but, as he said, after the first agreement had been signed with Newfoundland and the Minister was flying to Nova Scotia to negotiate with that Province, as quoted in The Globe and Mail of November 5, 1983, as the plane hit the runway in Halifax-
Mliss Campbell: It was Port Hawkesbury, not Nova Scotia.

It says Halifax here. But the quote is the main thing. It is the same as what Churchill said about nationalization, "When you scramble an omelette, you cannot unscramble it." Mr. Kirby must have been thinking of Mr. Churchill when he said:
Whatever happens now, what we've pulled off-restructuring the industry and at the same time creating a new federal fisheries policy-can never be undone.
That is what gives me concern. We have an immediate problem, and this is a quick legislative fix that 1 believe parliamentary history has proven does not work. Until more questions are answered in the committee, I am not optimistic, and 1 believe we have legitimate reasons to try to negotiate a better deal in Nova Scotia.

Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to ask the Hon. Member a question. 1 share some of his concerns about the policy behind the Bill. Without getting into that at this point, 1
simply want to know how he can base his argument by saying that the federal Government is responsible for the problems in the fishing industry? It was the federal Government, under the former Minister of Fisheries, which told the companies and the Provinces of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland in particular not to overfish in the spring of 1981. Despite this advice they overfished and the Governments of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia were in a war in competition for the northern cod. They opened up some new plants against the advice of the federal Government. It is the companies and the two provincial Governments, particularly the Government of Newfounland, that are responsible for the overfishing in 1981. That is what led to the high inventories when interest rates went over 25 per cent. How can the Member say that the federal Government is responsible when it told the companies and the Governments not to do that?
Mr. Speaker, I said earlier that I had to catch a plane.
Oh, oh!

There should be no oh, ohs. I said that 1 was not going to review all the history since it does not resolve the problem. But it is another concern which I have. In his speech the Minister stated that we are setting up a FishCan Corporation-this is where I disagree with Mr. Kirby-because so far there is no new federal fishery policy. It is the same fish policy that got us into the problem. Does the Member believe that creating a new corporation will resolve the problem?
The fact of the matter is that one can read the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, The Globe and Mail or the speech by the Member for South Shore. With respect to the fishing quota, restrictions in the St. Lawrence, the restrictions on licenses to boats, on the size of boats, everyone in the fish trade, including Mr. Nickerson of Nickerson and Sons which went under, National Sea Foods which went under, and the three companies in Newfoundland which have closed the three plants, knew that the former Minister of Fisheries and Oceans had a bias against modern fishing operations. He wanted political interference to help support his fishing communities in New Brunswick. He had archaic policies. We now have a new FishCan Corporation, and there has been no indication so far that the policy will change. Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I had many other questions to ask the Hon. Member, but he is in the habit of hitting and running. I am sorry that he could not stay. I will just repeat that his assumption, like that of the Hon. Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) when he spoke earlier this week, that the federal Government is to blame for the demise of the fishing industry in Atlantic Canada, is wrong. The policy of the former Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and of the federal Government before the Kirby process started was one that would not have led to the problems in the fishing industry we have seen if they had been followed by the fishing companies, the main actors in the industry, and the Governments of
November 17, 1983

Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. Rightly or wrongly, 1 cannot question the political motives of provincial Governments. 1 am not entitled to do that as a member of the public. If they want to pursue a certain political action, that is fine. They should bear the consequences of what they do however. The fact is that the Government of Newfoundland was in competition with the Government of Nova Scotia. When 1 say the Government 1 mean the two provincial economies which were in competition for the northern cod and for groundfish. They overfished. They overdid it. The companies did this against the advice of the former Minister of Fisheries, and they got themselves into a jam.
One cannot ignore the fact that the union which Mr. Cashin directs in Newfoundland is not only a union. I guess he would accept the definition himself that it is a social and political movement as well which had the industry on strike in 1980 or 1981. Do you expect that to be without cost? Do you expect to have a total industry in a province on strike without any cost? Are they accepting the responsibility for that? It seems to me that when you put an industry on strike you should know that there are consequences at the end, and the consequences can be bankruptcy, failure. I do not think those people have accepted that responsibility. I am not suggesting they were wrong to go on strike.
Oh, oh!

No, I am not. It is not for me to decide. When you go on strike and stifle an industry for about half a year, you have to accept the responsibility for what you do. They should accept the responsibility for what they did. Nevertheless, we are in this situation now.

Mr. Speaker, we are studying Bill C-170, an Act to authorize investment in and the provision of financial assistance to the Atlantic Fisheries for the purpose of restructuring certain fishing enterprises. This afternoon, 1 will not deal with the Bill because, in my opinion, there is no need for such a Bill, we should not have to study the Bill, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (M. De Bane) should not have had to introduce it in the House because, in the winter of 1981-82, there were ways to cope with the situation in fisheries. The problem is that, at the time, the Government decided to have the situation in fisheries reviewed by a group whose political master was not the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Normally, such issues come under the structural and political responsibility of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. The Government decided to involve a group which would analyze the situation and make recommendations.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the group made a very serious mistake. It made the mistake of wanting to re-invent the wheel. It made a mistake when it listened approvingly to many interested parties in Atlantic fisheries, mostly the large companies and, in certain cases, especially the Government of Nova
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act Scotia which kept saying that everything done by the federal Governement in fisheries was bad, the kind of comments we have heard from the Official Opposition in the past two or three days. Anything done about stock management or about quota management was bad because that was interference in an industry which ought to have much more freedom. In my opinion, the Kirby Task Force naively swallowed that premise. It is partly for that reason that we are experiencing problems today, yet another analysis of the fisheries problems, an attempt at re-inventing the wheel, while we did have the statutory, legal, financial and political means to solve the problem of fisheries in 1981-82, notwithstanding the origin of the crisis.
I would rather not delve too deeply into those issues. Mr. Speaker, the problem with Bill C-170 is not the Bill itself, that is only part of a more serious and much more wide-ranging problem. I am wondering whether there is an orientation and a philosophy in the field of fisheries, or whether we are simply faced with bits and pieces produced by a committee whose approach has been to compromise with everybody. One can compromise to the point where one's statements no longer mean anything.
There is nothing wrong with seeking a consensus, but in a field such as fisheries we just cannot ignore the fact that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is the federal Department which must be most politically aware, in the sense that it reacts to the people because, through that Department-and possibly it is the only one-the federal Government is related directly to the people. There is not other level of Government. A fisherman knows that he gets his permit from the federal Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, and he knows which jurisdiction, which sectors of fisheries come under the federal or provincial constitutional authority. It is therefore a highly political field.
So, Mr. Speaker, we do need a clear orientation and philosophy in the field of fisheries. And I happen to think that until the winter of 1982, we had a coherent federal policy in the field of fisheries. However, from that time on, it was decided to follow another path. As I said earlier, it turned out to be an attempt at re-inventing the wheel and to swallow faulty premises, therefore the analyses were wrong. And yet, we could have taken a different approach instead of introducing Bill C-170 and its famous concept of restructuration.
There is one thing which must be pointed out. The Hon. Member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell) did so this morning. The Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons) spoke in support of the Bill and, although I disagree with some of his conclusions, as I disagree with the Bill, I find it extremely difficult to endorse the Bill. Still, in his definition of the problem, he said something which I found very interesting.

When the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons) at one point said that the banks had the Government in

November 17, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
a corner-I am paraphrasing what he said, but he said we have to do something-he was right. He defined it well. I believe that, very naively someone early in this crisis, once the Kirby process started, intentionally or unintentionally, gave signals to the banks that there was an easy way out for this, that this matter could be easily solved, that this restructuring concept could fix things. I think that was very naive. I think that is where the mistake happened.
I notice in the Minister's speech as reported at page 28850 of Hansard for November 14, that he said this:
History will note that in the case of all those commercial undertakings which I mentioned-National Sea Products Ltd., Nickerson, Fishery Products, Penny & Sons, North Atlantic, Pecheurs-Unis-hundreds and thousands of creditors agreed to wait and did not take any action because they knew that we were trying to find a solution.
They agreed to wait. Were they asked to wait? They must have been. Their creditors must have been asked to wait. Who asked them? Was it the political authority that asked them or was it Doctor Kirby?
Then we say that there was no private capital. There was no way for private capital to be involved in the restructuring. There was never any attempt to solve the matter through private capital. Private capital will not buy the debts of the bank. Private capital will not come to a company that is going bankrupt and say, "Hey, Sir, 1 am going to buy the company and take on your debts". Private capital will say, "Fine. Let the bank get a receiver, put the plant in receivership and then we will see if we will buy." Normally, I thought that was the rule of the game. The banks puts the outfit into receivership; then private capital may look at it. That is when we can ask a private entrepreneur, "Do you have a restructuring plan? What kind of assistance do you want from the Government?" Then we decide what kind of assistance to give. As soon as a signal was given that there was an easy way out or that the Government would not let the industry collapse or go bankrupt, of course the banks and others had the Government in the corner. That is a lousy way to proceed, in my view. It will be disastrous for the future, not only of the fishing industry but of other industries as well. If this Bill goes through and if the restructuring goes through, I am afraid there will be further demands for restructuring. Other banks will come around and say that in other sectors they cannot go on, that the Government cannot let them collapse.
There were ways to deal with difficult situations in the fishery before. The Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) were correct when they said that the federal Government could not just let the companies go bankrupt with their high inventories and that prices could have been depressed through panic sales by receivers, particularly in the United States. 1 agree. Anyone who knows anything about the fishery knows that there were ways to deal with it. We dealt with that in 1969 and 1974. The Fisheries Price Support Board has the legal expertise and is the financial mechanism by which to do it. I am told that all the companies had to do was sign a piece of paper. If 1 recall
correctly how it was done, there was a confirmation by the bank that it could not hold the inventory any longer. Then the Fisheries Price Support Board could finance the inventory, provide a loan guarantee and hold it until the price was acceptable. That is the way to proceed. That is the way to ensure an inventory is not sold by a receiver in a panic situation. Why was that not done? I know that was tried before they set up this new process of reinventing the wheel. Why did they not do that? That is what they should have done.

Mr. Speaker, we are told-and I am quite willing to believe the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans when he says this because, even though he is sponsoring Bill C-170, he is not responsible for this situation because he did not appoint the Kirby task force, he was not the one to choose its policy or to choose or even negotiate restructuring nor was he the one to negotiate and develop the restructuring plan-but when we are told that these corporations will operate at arm's length from the Government, I am quite ready to believe it, but whether we believe it or not, or whether all the Members of the House agree, it is not important. When a bill is passed and the Government acquires equity in a company, the matter of whether or not there will be political influence is not important.
However, Mr. Speaker, only two years ago, the Government tried to transform the Canada Development Corporation into a policy instrument for Canada. 1 was in agreement with that philosophy and with the fact that, if the Canadian Government held 45 or 49 per cent equity in the Canada Development Corporation, the Canadian Parliament should have something to say about the policies of this corporation, but there was an outcry at this suggestion and we had to reverse our decision. If we were trying to influence this corporation, why not do the same for this other one? I do not know which minister will be responsible for the equity in these companies one, two or three years from now. It could be someone who will want to make decisions and manage the company and who will put a stop to this. Once Bill C-170 gives the power to sell or buy shares, who can stop a future minister from doing so? Mr. Speaker, there is no danger for the federal Government to be judge and party with regard to fisheries decisions in the future. One of the reasons why the federal Government earned respect in the field of fisheries in the past is that, when the constitutional jurisdiction over fisheries was put into question, the fishing communities gave us their support; it is also because the federal Government has always acted as a an objective referee between small and large companies, between various fleets and between the provinces. But the moment we are no longer considered as an objective referee, because we have shares in companies such as National Sea Products Limited and in the other company in Newfoundland, no wonder the fishing communities are getting very nervous. People are wondering how the ground fish industry is going to survive, particularly in
November 17, 1983

New Brunswick, in Prince Edward Island, in certain parts of Quebec and Nova Scotia, because not only are we going to have a giant as we had before-we are used to having giants- but now it is going to be a giant owned mostly by the federal Government and the Government of Nova Scotia. Suffice to point out that the agreement with Nova Scotia had hardly been signed that already pressure was brough to bear so that Nova Scotia companies might gain wider access to the ground fish resources in the gulf. Of course, Mr. Speaker, because we can already see a link between the political interest of the new company established for Nova Scotia and the federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans, when the Minister also says that the new company will look after marketing or will offer its marketing services to the independents.

I am talking here not only about plant owners. There are hundreds of communities in Atlantic Canada which have independent processors, independently-owned fish plants. They carry with them the community-fishermen, people who service the industry and people who work in the plants. There is a community spirit behind these independents. To suggest to independent processors that the federal Government, which provides a marketing regime or structure for wheat, dairy products and milk through the Canadian Dairy Commission, and for eggs, poultry and other products, will tell them that when it comes to fish they will have to go through a super company in Nova Scotia if they need marketing assistance is really very offensive and just about an insult. That is an abdication of the federal Government's responsibility in the marketing of fish, and that should not be allowed to stand as policy.
I was hopeful Dr. Kirby would come up with a clear idea about marketing. As 1 just said, we have a structure in our system for wheat, milk, poultry and other products. Why can we not have it for fish? What is the ideological sclerosis that we cannot have it for fish?

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the political aspect and dimensions of that restructuration cannot be ignored. I said that it was an indication of a more serious problem, and fishing communities are wondering what is going on when all of a sudden the federal Government is concerned about saving the large companies, what is going on when the federal Government buys $14 million worth of Canada Development Corporation shares. A company cannot properly administer its own business, it reaches a point where its operations are down, practically bankrupt, yet the Canadian Government gets into the picture and buys $14 million worth of shares. I for one cannot see any logic in that, yet there is no money to give grants to fishermen to buy boats, there is no money to solve the problem created by the over capacity of herring seiners. I do not know-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I note from the signal of the Chair that the Hon. Member's time is
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act expiring. I am sure the House would be prepared to grant him extended time so that he can complete this most interesting speech.

Mr. Speaker, whether one agrees with his views or not, the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) is always very charitable.

Mr. Speaker, in any case, I shall be brief. I have already said that the restructuring bill reflects a greater problem and that I wondered whether there has really been a clear strategy for fisheries since the Government decided to create the Kirby Commission. We really have to wonder whether there is a strategy. Sometimes, to be kind and not say that there is a bad one, I tell myself that maybe there is none. In my opinion, when we decided to reinvent the wheel in 1982, we may have rendered the federal Government and the federal fisheries policy completely powerless.
I have already mentioned the problem of herring seiners. There seems to be an excess capacity of herring seiners. Early in August, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans announced a policy stating that the solution would be to reduce the landing capacity. Leaving aside the issue of whether we agree or not, let us look at the mechanism suggested by the Minister. In my opinion, this mechanism is the most unfair that I have ever seen ever since I came to this House, a mechanism through which herring fishermen will be able to purchase the quota of another fisherman without the Government doing anything to reduce the landing capacity. Mr. Speaker, this goes against all the earlier policies developed for fisheries, which were aimed mainly at encouraging independent fishermen as much as possible; this means that a wealthy fisherman, who has already had good years in herring fishing and who has paid back the loan on his boat, will be able to purchase other quotas, while someone who came to the fishing industry a bit later, who is necessarily younger-
During the lean years!

-during the lean years, as noted by my colleague for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr), will be able to buy what? He can buy nothing because he has no money. He owes money on his boat. He has just come into the fishing industry. He is young. He has a new boat. He has not seen the good years of herring fishing. What can he do? All he can do is to sell his quota. How can he sell his quota without selling his boat? He is stuck.
Mr. Speaker, this is the most unfair policy ever developed, but once more, I cannot say that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is wholly responsible for this concept, as once again was developed by the Kirby Commission. I wonder how someone who knew anything about the fishing industry could have developed such a concept! Here also, the Kirby report states:

November 17, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act There should not be any subsidies for fishing vessels. Mr. Speaker, the fishing vessel subsidy program was the means through which independent fishermen were able to acquire boats. Today, in New Brunswick, for instance, over 90 per cent of all fishing vessels are owned by individual fishermen and not by companies, thanks largely to the fishing vessel subsidy program. This year, this program has not yet been in effect. [English]
I hope that the Government and all Members of Parliament will look very seriously at this restructuring proposal, consider the broader problems and examine very carefully what went on since January, 1982. I hope we will consider the systems put in place then to deal with this kind of problem to see why they were not used rather than invent new concepts which gave a signal to the banks that we would not let the companies go bankrupt.
In conclusion 1 say that I was ready to accept the idea of an abnormal approach in Newfoundland. I was ready to accept that in the case of Newfoundland because of the relative importance of the fishery to the provincial economy. I do not think the economy of Newfoundland could absord any more shocks. Broadly speaking, there was justification politically for the Government to do something abnormal in the case of Newfoundland, to look at the problem there differently. The high unemployment rate in that Province is a chronic problem. That Province is isolated geographically. Its economy depends very much on the groundfish industry in particular.
In the case of Nova Scotia, no one will convince me that there was a need for an abnormal approach to restructure, if restructuring was necessary at all in Nova Scotia, other than to be involved in a political reaction because of the fact that Newfoundland would be receiving a restructured industry. Is the only reason for a restructuring proposal for Nova Scotia, an abnormal or different approach by Government, the competition between the two provincial economies as to who will get the fish? If that is the case, the restructuring proposals for Nova Scotia do not make any sense. They are a threat to the groundfish industry all around the Gulf of St. Lawrence in the Provinces of Quebec, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.
As I speak today, people who own fish plants in the groundfish industry or whose plants involve an important element of groundfish are not sure whether they will have to abandon them. If that happens, the Government of Canada, along with the provincial Governments concerned, will have participated in the demise of an industry all around the Gulf of St. Lawrence. In the case of Newfoundland, that will not necessarily be the result. The threat in the Newfoundland situation is not the same as in Nova Scotia. It is not a mere coincidence that in the agreement signed with Nova Scotia there is a paragraph which deals with access to more groundfish in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. I believe that the new company, the federal Government and the provincial Government in Nova Scotia will try to establish a link between the federal fisheries policies and the management of this company. That is inevitable. When people assure me that that will not happen, I
believe that it is not their intention, but 1 cannot accept that as a political answer because I do not know what the political situation will be next spring, next fall or a year from now. 1 do not know who the Minister will be at that time. I do not know if the link will go much further than a mere peek at what management does. It may go much beyond that. This will mean that independent processors will not be able to obtain financing. They will not be able to maintain their marketing position because of the presence of super companies owned by the Governments, and the Bank of Nova Scotia.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct one or two short questions to the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) who just made a most interesting speech. He made a number of interesting comments which will certainly have to be looked at as the debate progresses, particularly when we get to the committee stage of this Bill. He said there are other ways in this Bill to go about solving the problems of the deep sea fishery of the Atlantic Provinces. That is a rough paraphrase, but he did say that. He then went on to put all the blame on Kirby and the banks. Obviously he feels very strongly against the method the Government has adopted and he spoke most eloquently in that regard. If there are ways other than the restructuring Bill now before the House, how does he intend to vote on this Bill in its present form?

First, Mr. Speaker, when I said that there were other ways, I did mention, in the case of preventing the collapse of prices through a panic selling of inventory, that the Fisheries Price Support Board could have provided loan guarantees, as has been done previously in times of crisis to make sure that the inventory would not be sold at panic prices. That is one of the ways of dealing with the problem.
What I said in my speech, and what I do believe strongly, is that when the crisis occurred in the fall of 1981 and the early winter of 1982, but particularly in the fall of 1981, there were other ways to deal with the problem. Once the Government, either politically or through officials, or the Kirby Commission, started giving signals to the banks and everyone else concerned that the Government would not let the industry collapse or go bankrupt, then I am not sure if any approach other than this one could have been used.
At the time, Mr. Speaker, 1 think there was a restructuring process occurring, not only for the fishing industry but for other industries. This would occur in a case where a plant was being sold by a receiver, as occurred in my constituency in the spring of 1983. The receiver put a plant up for sale. The bank lost a good deal of its money and, as well, many people lost a good deal of money. A new group came in and said that they would like to buy this plant if the Government would give it assistance and provide the means. The Government, through the DREE Program, provided some assistance, and the plant is now in operation. That is a restructuring process but it is one that does not give off signals that everybody around the plant will be bailed out. 1 think that that is probably what went wrong in this situation.
November 17, 1983

The Hon. Member must be aware that according to news reports, the Canada Development Corporation has apparently sold its shares in Fisheries Products to the federal Government for $14 million. In this case, Fisheries Products in Newfoundland run their company into the ground for whatever reason and the result is that the Canada Development Corporation sells its shares in Fisheries Products to the Government for $14 million.
In answer to the Hon. Member's question, I am not sure that there is any other way to go about it now, but there was another way in the spring of 1982. As to the question of how 1 will vote on this Bill, frankly, I have not yet made up my mind.
I will listen to the debate very, very carefully. I said in my speech that 1 found it extremely difficult to support the Bill. I will reflect and 1 will listen to debate, after having added my speech to the debate, before I decide how I will vote.
I must tell the Hon. Member that one of the things that concerns me is the way his Party is trying to sit on the fence on this issue. The Hon. Member has not yet spoken and he normally does not sit on the fence. I hope I hear him speak from one side of the fence only. Either Conservative Members are for this kind of intervention or they are not, because there are some powers in this Bill that go way beyond what we were doing with Canagrex, with Canadair and with other Crown agencies, and the Hon. Member's Party attacks us all the time for those. I hope that I will hear that the Hon. Member for St. John's East takes a sincere position that comes from one side of the fence or the other.

Mr. Speaker, with the kind of opposition the Hon. Member has given this Bill, he does not need any help from this side of the House.
1 would like to ask the Hon. Member one question. Many of the restructured plants will require access to the Gulf in order to get at those surplus groundfish stocks. That is a question that is very dear to the heart of the Hon. Member and I have the scars to prove it. I ask the Hon. Member if he would support opening the Gulf to deep sea trawlers so that they can catch that surplus stock and not allow it to die.

Mr. Speaker, first, the wide-ranging assertion of the Hon. Member that there is a surplus of groundfish in the Gulf is wrong. There is no surplus of goundfish in the Gulf. There is a temporary surplus situation with redfish, which is a kind of groundfish, but it is only a temporary situation. I know that the Hon. Member reads biological reports very carefully, as I do. Perhaps he should have read those reports more carefully in 1979, but I know that he reads them very carefully now. He should know that this is a temporary situation and that the assertion he makes that there is a surplus of groundfish in the Gulf is simply not factual.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, 1 have never been dogmatic on this issue. He must remember the way I approached the question in 1979. The issue here is whether or not the problem in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia with the offshore fleets is caused by a shortage of fish. That is the real question. Anyone who looks at the facts cannot honesty say that the problems
Adjournment Motion
are caused by a shortage of fish. Newfoundland has tripled its landings of groundfish since 1977. Nova Scotia has increased its landings of fish by over 100 per cent. New Brunswick is the only Province that has yet to recapture its fish landings from the early 1970s and the late 1960s.
The issue here is one of fairness. Do we give all of the fish to the regions-no, I will say fleets instead of regions because 1 do not like to talk about this situation in interprovincial terms. Do we give more fish to the fleets that have tripled their landings, or do we preserve the Gulf of St. Lawrence for those fleets that have no other place to fish, do not have the boats to go offshore and can only fish in the Gulf? I approach this issue, Mr. Speaker, from the basic position of fairness. The resources of the Gulf should be kept for those who have access only to the Gulf and do not have boats capable of going offshore. The other fleets which have tripled their landings have problems other than the problem of a shortage of fish. They should address those problems.
While 1 am on that topic, Mr. Speaker, let me remind Hon. Members that I said in my speech that unions have a great deal of things to say on these matters and they tend to be socio-political movements as well as unions. They should bear the responsibility for the fact that the offshore fleet is apparently not viable now. It is not making profits and it is in deficit. Apparently its way of fishing with offshore trawlers is not a good way to fish. The offshore fleet should solve the problem in ways other than asking us who have access only to the Gulf to be sacrificed in order to subsidize their non-viable operations.
