speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just heard a most interesting and eloquent speech made by the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau). In reply to two very simple questions, he told us in one instance that he is very much opposed to this Bill, has reservations about it and is keeping an open mind on it. That means of course, when one reads through that rhetoric, that if the Bill re-emerges at third reading in its present form, he will vote against it if he is to be consistent.
Second, with regard to surplus groundfish stocks in the Gulf, the Hon. Member would have us believe that there are no surplus stocks, and that would mean that the work of our federal Fisheries Department in rebuilding these stocks over the past number of years has been a total failure. That of course is not the case and he knows that.
He also knows, better than anyone in the House, that the capacity of the Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick fleets is such that they cannot catch all of the fish in the Gulf. That is a fact. The stock has grown beyond the capacity of the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island fleets and the Hon. Member knows that. He knows that full well, and he also knows, Mr. Speaker, that these stocks, if not caught, will die. I think he also knows, because he was the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries for-

Mr. Speaker I rise on a point of order. I have the highest respect for my predecessor as Minister of Fisheries, but may I remind the Hon. Member that we are discussing a restructuring Bill that deals with some failing companies. We are not discussing the fishing plans for the next year. That is a totally unrelated matter, and I believe he would recognize that the topic he was discussing, while most important, has no bearing upon the Bill that we are discussing.

Mr. Speaker, I am really and truly surprised by that intervention because the question of Gulf stocks is one that is critical to this Bill. I prefaced my remarks by saying that if some of the restructured plants are not given access to that Gulf stock, they cannot survive. That is their whole raison d'etre. The plants on the south coast of Newfoundland, for example, that are very much a part of the restructured Newfoundland company, must have access to that Gulf stock if they are to survive and prosper, and the Minister knows that only too well. If he does not know that, then I would say that
we are in worse shape than I thought in terms of the administration of the fisheries of this country.
I did not want to get carried away with the question of Gulf stocks, Mr. Speaker, because that is a decision the Minister will have to make. And he will have to learn to live with that politically, as I did.
Oh, oh!

I hear the laughter of the Hon. Member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell) and the Hon. Member for Gloucester. But they cannot have their cake and eat it too, because we will be watching very carefully at third reading stage of this Bill to see if they are prepared to put their money where their mouths are. Very simply, Mr. Speaker, they cannot have it both ways.
The Hon. Member for Gloucester went out of his way in his speech to blame the banks, the Kirby task force and the unions for the mess which brought us to the point where we had to bring forth this Bill. And, of course, he blamed the provincial Governments as well. He blamed everyone but the Government, of which he was a member at one time by being Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries for two or three years.
Point of order, Mr. Speaker.
I did not interrupt the Member when he was speaking, and these spurious points of order-[DOT]
Order.
1 know my hon. friend always wants to be accurate. Unfortunately, I was never the Parliamentary Secretary to any Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
That is not a point of order.

That is not a point of order. Even if I have made a mistake in that regard, he has been Parliamentary Secretary to just about every other Minister. That is perhaps the only one he has not been assigned to. In any event, if he was not the Parliamentary Secretary, it is a known fact that he was extremely close to the previous Minister of Fisheries and Oceans who comes from an adjoining constituency or from the same part of New Brunswick as the Hon. Member.
The Hon. Member for Gloucester proceeded to blame everyone but the Government of Canada. The facts are very simple. When we declared our 200-mile limit in 1977 there was a great aura of expectation, and rightly so, because we were going to get control of our fisheries. There was also a great opportunity, which was missed at that time, an opportunity to put our house in order. Instead of seizing that opportunity, we went on a binge in terms of over-extending to the point at which we got ourselves in very deep trouble.
November 17, 1983

I will bring you to the point, Mr. Speaker, of the appointment of the Kirby task force, forgetting what happened in between, and the problems which plagued the industry prior to 1977 with the rape of the fishing grounds by the international fleets and the failure of ICNAF to address itself to that problem. We will skip over all that and bring ourselves to the point at which the Kirby task force was appointed by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) in January of 1982.
The plants were failing one by one during the summer of 1981. Why? They were failing and closing during the summer of 1981 because of a number of things over which this Government had some control, one being high interest rates. High interest rates of 22 per cent were coming about at a time when there was a change in the market in terms of the strengthening of the U.S. dollar, which made our European competitors more competitive. There was a change in consumer habits in the United States resulting from the fact that poultry was becoming more competitive with fish in the marketplace. All these things came together at a time when we had a monetarist policy in this country of 22 per cent interest rates. The companies could not sustain their inventories and the banks had to move in to keep those companies alive.
We made the plea during the summer of 1981. 1 made plea after plea in the form of telegrams to the Prime Minister and to the former Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to act before it was too late. But nothing was done. The result is that we are paying for it today. Nothing was done until a final realization on the part of the Government reaching right into the Prime Minister's office in the winter of 1981-82, which resulted in the appointment of the Kirby task force.
What happened then? We know what happened. The Kirby task force found itself getting in deeper and deeper, and the report was delayed to the point that when the report did come down, there was no reference made to the question of restructuring. What we have here is not what was contained in the Kirby task force report.
Notwithstanding how we got into this mess, Mr. Speaker, 1 want to make one thing very clear to the Hon. Member for Gloucester and to this House. This Bill is absolutely critical to the survival of the deep water fisheries in the province of Newfoundland. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. de Bane) will receive no quarrel from me on that. What I do have to argue against and warn against is the danger that this Bill may somehow be presented as a panacea, as some kind of magic wand which will solve all the problems of the deep water fishery. We have no agreement in Nova Scotia. I do not know where that will lead. However, we do have a signed agreement with Newfoundland which not only has the support of the Newfoundland Government, but has the support of the Fishermen's Union and the principal creditors. I say to you, Sir, that if the industry is to survive, then the Minister must have the authority to proceed with this Bill. That speaks to the question of urgency.
The Minister knew all this in July of this year, when he proceeded unilaterally, when he could not get an agreement with Newfoundland. He certainly knew in September, when he
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act finally did get an agreement on September 28, that it was a matter of some urgency. He knew back in the summer of this year that he would require legislation. He was warned that legislation would be required. He could not proceed without it. This was a major departure from normal procedure. It was a major venture for the Government of Canada, and it had to have statutory authority to proceed in this way. Yet, Sir, we were not presented with the Bill until October 31, one full month after the agreement with Newfoundland. We were then told we had to move very quickly. This was a matter of great urgency.
1 do not really question the urgency; however, instead of proceeding with the Bill, it was allowed to stand for a week. Finally, when the Government did decide to move with second reading of the Bill, we had one day's debate, and at the eleventh hour, without any explanation, the Government decided to proceed the next day with an Opposition day. 1 still do not understand why we did not continue with the debate on Monday and Tuesday. If we had done so, this Bill would now either be before the committee or back in the House for third reading. In that case the Minister would not have the problems he now has. I do not blame the Minister entirely, although one would expect he would have a little more influence on his colleague, the Government House Leader. If he was not able to exercise his influence successfully, surely he could have called on his colleague, the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston), who chaired the committee which brought about this whole affair in the first place. I am sure that between the two of them they could have persuaded the Government House Leader to get on with this Bill, to get on with the very urgent and important business of restructuring.
However, the Bill ignores, and the Minister deliberately ignores, some of the serious problems facing the industry, for example, fleet replacement. Who is going to pay for the replacement of the trawlers? We have 140 trawlers in the Atlantic Provinces with an average age of 14 to 15 years. Many of these trawlers are over 20 years of age. They have to be replaced with new equipment. That is a major financial undertaking. That is one of the problems which the new company will have to face, and very quickly, because that was one of the things which brought the existing companies virtually to the point of bankruptcy. They had to face up to these questions in addition to carrying the burden of debt placed on them by virtue of the high interest rate monetarist policy of the Government. Who is going to pay for these new trawlers? Is the Government going to set up a new Crown corporation to pay for and operate them and therefore totally control the harvesting sector, then, in turn, sell the catches to the giant companies? In other words, it would buy from one of its companies and sell to another one of its companies.
We are dealing with an industry directly responsible for the lives of about 70,000 or 80,000 people in the Atlantic Provinces and Quebec. It is as important to us as the Crow legislation is to western Canada. It is critically important to us

November 17, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act in Newfoundland. Yet no reference is made to the plight of the inshore fishermen. I would have expected the Hon. Member for Gloucester to have addressed that problem. God knows, we have about 48,000 inshore fishermen in the Atlantic region if you classify them as those who operate boats under 100 feet in length. The Minister knows we have serious problems with the inshore fishery regarding income and quality control. This year the inshore fishery in many parts of the Province of Newfoundland was a failure. Yet we still do not have any policy designed to address the problems facing the inshore fishermen which will give them an income they can depend upon and the opportunity to compete and survive. The average inshore fisherman in Newfoundland earns about $8,000 a year and works very hard for it. He has to content himself with unemployment insurance to get him through the rest of the winter.
There is no question in my mind that the moment this Bill is passed, and it will pass in this form or an amended form, someone will have to face these very serious questions of fleet replacement and our inshore fishermen, because you cannot deal with one at the expense of the other. I listened very carefully to the Hon. Member for Gloucester. He talked about the fact there was no underlying philosophy, that the Government was responding to task force kinds of responses in a dispirited way. On that score he was dead right, because that is very much a part of the problem. The Minister knows that full well because he inherited it, just as I did during my brief tenure as Minister. But at least we made an attempt to put our House in order. One of the first things we did as a Government was to order a total review of fisheries policy to try to get around some of the mistakes of the past, to try to get some kind of philosophy so that those depending upon the industry for their livelihood would know where it was going. That would deal with the question of fleet replacement, quality control and developing new markets. It would deal with the problems in developing new species and new markets for new species, which speaks to the whole question of research and development. All of these things were tragically ignored by this Government immediately it took office because it went right back to square one.
We put in place a total review of fisheries policy, which was immediately scrapped when the Liberal Government took over in 1980. We put in place a policy for rationalizing over-the-side sales, which at that time were chaotic. Both fishermen and Canadian processors would be able to take full advantage of this new marketing technique, but that policy was immediately undone by the incoming Government. We put in place a new salmon policy which called for the building of new hatcheries to preserve the Atlantic salmon. The only part of that policy followed through successfully by the Government was the conclusion of an international convention.
We are paying for these mistakes, Mr. Speaker, and paying dearly. We will continue to pay. What we have in front of us today is a Bill which is a direct result of the knee jerk, band-aid reactions of this Government to one problem after another facing the industry. 1 say to the Minister that the Bill
he has in front of him today is the only thing he can do right now. 1 do not agree with the Hon. Member for Gloucester. The Minister had no choice. There was no other way he could go, he had to save the industry. In order to do that, there had to be massive federal and provincial Government involvement as well as that of the creditors. It is all very well to dump all over the Bank of Nova Scotia, but it is going to carry its share of the new company as well. 1 have no grief for the bank or the other creditors, and there are other creditors, but they will have to work with the two levels of Government to ensure the viability of this company to the point where not only will they become economically viable and be able to stand on their own two feet and compete in the markets of the world, but to the point where they can be handed back to the private sector where they rightfully belong.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder how the Hon. Member for St. John's East can, on the one hand, express concern for the inshore fishery and, on the other, argue for increased access to the resources of groundfish in the Gulf of St. Lawrence by larger trawlers. Can he reconcile those two positions? 1 do not really think they can be reconciled.
Secondly, when he says that the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island fleets do not have the capacity to catch the groundfish in the Gulf, how does he arrive at that conclusion? Traditionally, we were fishing upwards of 60,000 tons of groundfish through the new Brunswick fleet alone.

That can be reconciled by information which is available to anyone in this country from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. It is available to the Hon. Member. If he was open-minded enough to make the inquiries, he would get the same information I was able to get. The fact is that the Hon. Member knows full well that is a trans-boundary stock anyway. He knows there are trawlers involved in catching that stock. He also knows full well-if he does not, he should-that there are plants on the South Coast and in parts of Nova Scotia which, if they do not have access to the surplus stocks- and I say "surplus" because the inshore fishermen must have first priority-then it is very questionable in most cases whether they can be viable, and in some cases they cannot survive.

Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows, I was at one time the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans so I know a little bit about it. As he and I both realize, one of the best warehouses is the sea but once a fish is caught, if it is properly taken care of, it is one of the most nutritious and best food products man can consume. Does he not think it has been a pretty poor marketing job?
I cannot agree with the former Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment.
It used to be fisheries and forestries, and then we made it the environment.

That is right. When it became the Department of the Environment, fisheries became a mere service
November 17, 1983

within the Department of the Environment. That was taking place at a critical time in the growth of the industry. That is part of the problem as well. I am glad the Minister gave me a chance to put that on the record.
He talks about the fact that the ocean is probably one of the best storage facilities for fish. The difference is that if the fish stay in the ocean, they die. If they are caught and kept in cold storage, they are there to be marketed over a period of three months. The Minister put his finger on a very important problem which is going to be one of the major problems facing the new company. If we do not get access to the European market for groundfish these companies cannot survive. The Minister knows that full well and 1 am glad he gave me the opportunity to put that on the record.

Mr. Speaker, the Department of Environment was created when I was with the Minister of Fisheries. It was not put in force until afterwards. It did not take over fisheries. There was still the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry at that time.
We know that when you catch the fish from the sea or from fresh water it is a product that can be used in many societies all over the world. I am accused of trafficking too much of it. I find in many instances our fish does not reach those people in the condition that it should. Mr. Speaker, that is bad marketing. This is what I am pointing out. I just returned from the World Food and Agricultural Organization meeting. I chaired the meetings attended by Ministers of Agriculture and Fishery. A lot of them in the Commonwealth countries have dual capacity and authority. Fisheries was one of their main topics. They are concerned about their own fisheries and needing assistance from countries like Canada that, they feel, have the know-how in conservation and the catching of fish. We know that we can improve that in Canada. I am sure the Hon. Member agrees.
We need a "Fishagrex".

The Hon. Minister of Fisheries says we need a "Fishagrex". Here is a product that we need to be distributed in the world. We need it to be marketed in a fashion that it can be put on many people's dinner and supper tables in such a fashion that they can afford to eat it. I am sure that if it is improved in the fashion that my colleague, the Hon. Minister of Fisheries (Mr. De Bane), wants it to be, the fisheries can become the fisheries that we want it to be, one that will be economically viable and look after itself.
Will you repeat the question?
Mr. Speaker, I understood I could either ask a question or make statements.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak in support of Bill C-170 which is now before the House for
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act second reading. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) on Monday gave Members a detailed account of the measures that the Government proposes to take under this Bill. He has described very vividly the urgency of the situation which has caused the Government to introduce it.
Given that kind of introduction to Bill C-170, I have been somewhat disappointed in these last two days of debate to see that so many Members, rather than addressing themselves to the particular circumstances that now exist that give cause for this kind of legislation or to the fact that the legislation arises out of agreements that have been or are about to be reached with provincial Governments regarding the situation in the deep sea fishery, have instead applied themselves to talking about every kind of issue now affecting the Atlantic fishery, the inshore, deep sea, industrial, harvesting, processing side.
The Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) warned the Government that this Bill is not a panacea. It cannot solve all the problems. I want to inform the Hon. Member opposite that the Government has never claimed this Bill to be a panacea that will solve all the problems of the fishery. We have said instead that this Bill is designed to prevent what is clearly, and has been accepted on both sides of this House, a disaster. This point seems to have been lost as every Member seeks to raise before this House his own personal priority as far as the fishery is concerned.
I intend to stick to the subject matter at hand. The deep sea sector of the fishery is the cornerstone of the fishing industry in Atlantic Canada. It is a sector which had sales in 1982 of $770 million, a sector which has meant jobs for 44,000 people, 20,000 fishermen and 24,000 plant workers. I ask Members to reflect for just a moment on what 44,000 jobs mean in a region as economically depressed as Atlantic Canada. More particularly, what do those jobs mean when you break them down to a few hundred in this community and a few hundred in that community? Regionally, the rate of unemployment is 25 to 30 per cent, but on a community basis where these jobs are located unemployment is sometimes tragically at 40, 50, 60, 75 per cent. That is what we are talking about, not every side issue that may be on somebody's personal agenda to be addressed using this Bill as an excuse.
When one relates the figures to the population of Atlantic Canada one can see the significance of these activities to the economy of the Atlantic region. In relative terms, the deep sea fishery is as important to the Atlantic Provinces as the automotive industry is to central Canada. This is not an expendable industry. It is too large, too central to the life of the Atlantic region. Beyond that it is too richly endowed with potential for us to allow it to go under.
When smaller companies and industries fall by the wayside, many times the effects can be contained and corrected without too much difficulty. The price of buying them out is oftentimes low enough to be tackled by private investors with relatively small resources. If a fast food franchise goes bankrupt, the communities in which they operate can absorb the shock.
When a giant like this one stumbles, the earth begins to shake. I assure you there have been tremors in recent months

November 17, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
in Atlantic Canada. The deep sea industry cannot be allowed to fall, because in doing so it would create havoc and chaos throughout the industry. Because of its size, because it is a giant and because of its financial situation we cannot look to private sources to put it back on its feet. The Government knows this. We have looked. The industry, and the banks in particular, know this. They have looked to no avail. That is the reason why in this instance it takes the combined efforts of provincial Governments, the federal Government, and private financial institutions to get this industry back on its feet. Quite simply it is not feasible in this case to let the companies go bankrupt and wait for some entrepreneur to come along and, at so many cents on the dollar, pick up the pieces, and perhaps only some of the pieces, while 44,000 people are displaced directly. Indirectly, many thousands more are displaced in the name of private enterprise at any cost. I believe in private enterprise but not at any cost.
Let me give Hon. Members an example of the burden we are talking about. It has been estimated by financial analyses that the two consolidated companies visualized under this Bill will have to generate capital expenditures in the order of a quarter of a billion dollars each over the next five years. That is what they need for fleet replacement, maintenance of their plant capital, for new equipment to improve their productivity and other purposes. These are the kinds of obligations private investors, if you can find them, would be facing. Given the current condition of the industry, one cannot be surprised that investors are not lining up for the opportunity to shoulder them. If this lack of investment appeal were likely to be a permanent condition, we would face a much different situation. We in the House would probably be considering some very different action. But the evidence tells us that the condition is not permanent. There are solid reasons for long-term optimism.
There are many reasons why the deep sea fishing industry is in trouble. Inherent weakness and inadequate potential are certainly not among them. I am not one of those, as 1 have seen to my disappointment Hon. Members opposite do, to stand in the House and suggest that somehow all the problems in the current crisis that besets the Atlantic fishery can be written down in ten easy explanations and attributed to the policy of a single government. Anyone who really knows anything about the Atlantic fishery and who is really interested in making some helpful observations in the House will say that it is one of the most complex problems because of its socio-economic nature-I emphasize socio-economic nature- and one of the most complex industries that exists in this country.
The jurisdiction in the fisheries is shared. It is provincial Governments, not the federal Government, that control licences. It is provincial Governments that say how many fish plants there should be, where they should be, how big they should be and what they should process. It is not the federal Government. If one wanted to be strictly technical and was more interested in jurisdiction than in responding to a very
real problem affecting human beings, we would say as federal Members that, if it is not under our jurisdiction, then let us toss this Bill aside, not discuss the problem and let the Provinces handle it. That is where negotiations began at the table. There were the Provinces, the industry itself, the banks and the federal Government. Only one player reached into his pocket to put money on the table. It was the federal Government. Why? Because we wanted to spend $200 million or more of taxpayers' money? Because we wanted to get into the business of processing fish because we believed we could do it better than the private sector, the Provinces or the banks? No. Quite frankly, if we were to list 100 activities in which we would want to become involved, the processing and fishery business would not even be on that list. But we are interested in people, and that is why this Bill is before the House and that is why it needs an urgent and quick passage.
Let us address ourselves to the Bill. What are the consequences of not proceeding with this legislation on an urgent basis? We will see continuing uncertainty in the Atlantic fishing industry and in the communities which, as I have tried to describe, are so vitally dependent on it. We will see a continuation of existing plant closures and possibly further closures and lay-offs. I believe we will see distress selling by companies facing financial difficulty, with serious consequences for independent producers who have managed so far to keep afloat. What does distress selling mean? It means that there are a handful of corporate giants that are in serious financial trouble and are technically bankrupt in many cases. If we do not provide an infusion-not a bail-out of cash-by way of equity, those giants who are in trouble will find it easy to take all of the fish that they have warehoused and dump it on the market at drastically reduced prices, driving those small independent private enterpreneurs, who have survived and made a dollar, into bankruptcy together with them. They will not be able to compete, and that would be a consequence of not moving with this Bill.
We would see increased difficulties for creditors. There are many small companies throughout Atlantic Canada that are owed millions of dollars in total. Those dollars will not be paid, driving yet many doezens of other small companies into bankruptcy.
Labour contracts are currently expiring. These can be renegotiated only after new management is put into place.
The independents have been expressing a great deal of concern about the notion of having a couple of super companies in which the Governments have equity. I want to say that I have a great deal of sympathy for those independent producers and small operations which have managed to survive the rough times and still make a dollar. They have every right and should be concerned, and I understand that. I do not say that their concerns are justified or that I believe for one second that the consequences they envisage will occur. However, I do have some sympathy, because anyone who has been able to survive the last three years in this industry only to see now a couple of large companies being created which they believe threatens their existence, has every right to be concerned.
November 17, 1983

However, I suggest that the removal of a major uncertainty facing the entire industry will have a positive effect on the independents. If the Governments had not acted to forestall the collapse of the large processors, the entire industry, including independent processors, would have been threatened with collapse.
The restructuring focuses on the restructuring of strategically important companies whose size and socio-economic importance are of industry-wide importance. The restructured companies will provide an urgently required stability that will be beneficial to the entire industry, including the independents. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has said in the House and elsewhere in Canada during the last few months that these large processing giants will not be allowed and will in fact be specifically instructed against taking any action that will have a negative impact on small independent processors.
Many Members opposite, as well as some on this side, have suggested that this Bill is in some way a bail-out of the Bank of Nova Scotia. The Bank of Nova Scotia has not been bailed out nor given preferential financial treatment. The bank still has substantial outstanding loans made to the companies concerned with restructuring and has agreed to convert a major portion of that debt to equity. It is not walking away from the table. It has very much a stake in ensuring that this restructuring works because it still has a substantial amount of capital tied up in the two companies that have been created.
I was pleased to see the Hon. Member for St. John's East stand in his place today and indicate that there is absolutely nothing more urgent before Members of the House than Bill C-170. The Hon. Member indicated that quick passage is essential to the economy of Newfoundland and indeed to the economy of Nova Scotia. The Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) spoke eloquently in presenting his views from where he sits and as he sees them. I was pleased to see that he so well recognizes the urgency of this Bill, fundamentally to deal with the problem as it exists today.
I am not going to debate how we got where we are today. The Hon. Member for St. John's East said, "We are where we are today because the federal Government has mismanaged the industry, but when I was Minister and my Government was in power we had taken bold new strides". But Mr. Peckford, I recall, during the 1980 election campaign said that he preferred the former Minister, who supposedly created all these problems, to the Hon. Member for St. John's East. It is interesting to note, Mr. Speaker, that both the Hon. Member for St. John's East and Mr. Peckford are members of the same Party. 1 recall campaigning in my riding and, to my delight, saying "Yes, 1 agree with Mr. Peckford. Let us get Romeo LeBlanc back on stream." It is not good enough to say simplistically that the problems have been caused by one administration. No one administration, no one level of Government, even if it wanted, can cope with the complexity of the Atlantic industry. That is why I say to Hon. Members that this Bill is not a panacea. This Bill does not pretend for a moment
Royal Assent
to deal with or attempt to resolve every problem, every item that needs to be debated. This Bill, only as a first step, will ensure that the deep sea industry does not collapse. This Bill will ensure that the capital required for equity taken by Governments to maintain that industry, to renew it, to retool it, is available. It will ensure proper management and a businesslike approach. Then, in a number of years we can divest ourselves as Governments of these companies and turn them back to the private sector, back to private investors and risk takers who are prepared to run a profitable organization. That is what this Bill does, I say again, not because we want to be here but because we have no other choice. And if we had any concern for the 44,000 people in Atlantic Canada who, believe me, if they knew and were aware this debate were taking place would listen with bated breath, with patience, and would pray that this House of Commons will move quickly to see this Bill pass second reading, go to committee and finally go through this House and to the Senate, and that is what we should do.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Parliamentary Secretary. We have not even formed a new company to save the Atlantic fishing industry and already the Parliamentary Secretary is talking about divesting the Government of ownership in that company. In view of the problems that communities such as Burin, Grand Bank, St. Lawrence and St. Anthony have had under private ownership, 1 wonder whether the Parliamentary Secretary may not fear, if this is turned back to private enterprise, that those same communities that were in fear of closing down permanently would not be in the same situation in the future? Would the Parliamentary Secretary answer the question about the community ownership and co-operatives in communities rather than turning them strictly back to free enterprise? Would the Parliamentary Secretary consider that an alternative to his haste to get rid of this company and put it back into private enterprise hands?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to respond to the Hon. Member opposite, I want to assure him that the reason for my remarks was not to indicate that we should try to pass the Bill today and sell the companies tomorrow, but rather to point out that the Government really has, as a first motive, no interest in being in the fish business for the sake of being in the fish business. The Government really has as a first motive no desire to say that we own X amount of equity in the fishing industry. The Government only has as a motive a social responsibility, a responsibility as an elected Government to respond to a very real need that affects a great number of people in Atlantic Canada.
1 want to say to the Hon. Member that to suggest that somehow when private capital is involved we run the risk of closures and people being negatively affected is really a philosophical question that we can address to any industry in Canada. The Hon. Member knows that his Party's position is one of public ownership wherever possible. I do not happen to share that view. My own view is that the private sector can do it best and can generate the greatest amount of wealth but that people sometimes fall between the cracks. That is where Government should be and that is where Government should step in, otherwise Government should not be there. This is an example. If you want to call it a crack, it is almost like the San Francisco fault line. But there is a heck of a big crack. Private capital is not available right now. We should move in but move in very clearly with the idea of running this company on a businesslike basis. That is why we said that if the company, if its board of directors, said if X or Y or B or C plant is not viable and it will close down, and if a Government wants that particular plant to stay open, then it is the Government, not
the company, that will pay the cost of keeping an unproductive plant open. I simply suggest that it be run on a businesslike basis and that when possible the Governments divest themselves of their equity position in these companies.

Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of comments to address to the Parliamentary Secretary. First, I can appreciate the importance of the Atlantic fishery. The fishermen. 1 am sure, have been under a lot of hardship lately. I fully intend to support this piece of legislation although I might not agree 100 per cent with all that has been said this afternoon. But in listening to the speeches that have been made today 1 have a little better understanding of what has been happening in the Atlantic fishery.
I would like to point out to the Parliamentary Secretary that during his speech he said that the fishery in Atlantic Canada was just as important as the automotive industry is in central Canada. 1 would like to extend that a little further by saying that the Crow rate was that important to the farmers of western Canada as well. I would have hoped that some of the Members would have given consideration to that at the time the same way as some Members in the New Democratic Party are now paying attention to this piece of legislation, and we will be giving some support to it.
Further, Mr. Speaker, I have been dealing with the Minister's office for some time trying to get resolved a fishing problem in my own constituency which has a freshwater fish industry. I can appreciate that the Minister has had a lot of his own personal time taken up with dealing with this piece of legislation and the larger fishing industries in Canada. I would like to see, as soon as this Bill is passed, the Parliamentary Secretary, if the Minister cannot find the time, join with me and some other Members in taking a very close look at the freshwater fishing industry which is getting into severe problems in places like northern Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in response to the Hon. Member's comments, I want to assure him that the Department, indeed, the Government, recognizes the great value, the activity that takes place in the freshwater fishery. I avail myself in my position as Parliamentary Secretary of the opportunity to travel west and to see firsthand some of the activities in western Canada. I can assure him that if 1 can be of any assistance to him in resolving problems he is experiencing, on behalf of the Minister 1 would be delighted to do so. 1 would be glad to sit down at any time with him, as would the Minister, I am sure, or his officials to discuss with the Hon. Member any problems he would like to bring to our attention.

Parliamentary Secretary will know, this Bill will restrict or limit provincial participation in transportation to 10 per cent. In other words, it will put very

severe limitations on a provincial Government or an agency of a provincial Government to buy up more than 10 per cent of a corporation, particularly if it is directly involved in transportation or that transportation is the major sector of it. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 apologize to my hon. colleague; 1 know the Messenger from the Senate is on his way. However, I need to put on the record an agreement which has been reached with my colleague, the Hon. Member for Yukon. Before I reached the agreement with the Hon. Member for Yukon, I spoke with the House Leader for the New Democratic Party.

Member for Hamilton Mountain knows that I was to undesignate Thursday, possibly, and to push it a little further ahead to allow more time for the committees to study the Supplementary Estimates. ed out that I alerted him earlier in the day that the committees had not had the opportunity to examine Supplementary Estimates (B) and that the result of the designation of the allotted days made by the Government House Leader today meant that Parliament would not have the opportunity to examine Supplementary Estimates (B). speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: FISHERIES-NEWFOUNDLAND REPRESENTATION IN CABINET. (B) AGREEMENT BETWEEN GOVERNMENT AND BANK OF NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 12, I again had the unfortunate experience of addressing a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). It was, of course, a complete waste of time. 1 do not know where his mind is but it is not with us here in the House of Commons. Today he is riding his umbrella pursuing the peace cause around the world and we wish him well at that. We wish him more success at that than he has had with our domestic concerns here in Canada.
I asked the Prime Minister, in the context of the economic crisis in Newfoundland with 43,000 Newfoundlanders unemployed or 19 per cent of the labour force, what steps he was
going to take in connection with the fishing industry. Of course, he has taken no steps. I asked him whether we will have a representative on the Cabinet from Newfoundland. 1 asked him if he would appoint to the executive council a Member from Newfoundland. There are seven of us here in the House. 1 am prepared, if necessary, to make the sacrifice in Order to help the people of Newfoundland. In any event, there are five Liberal Members and two Progressive Conservative Members elected to the House from Newfoundland. When the Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) formed his administration, both Conservative Members from Newfoundland were Members of the Cabinet. That is the kind of representation that Newfoundland then had in the House.
Today there is no representative from Newfoundland in the Cabinet of Canada and one of the Liberal backbenchers, the Hon. Member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception (Mr. Rooney), says that Newfoundland is actually doing much better without a Cabinet representative than it was doing when the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) was a Cabinet Minister. Now there is solidarity for you.
By the way, Mr. Speaker, there is opposite me today a young Hon. Member who might well, in 50 years or 60 years time, have sufficient experience and calibre to be a member of the Government of Canada and in the Cabinet.
The fact remains, Mr. Speaker, that we do not now have a representative from Newfoundland in the Government of Canada, nor will we, and we are suffering as a result of it. There are five representatives from Newfoundland here and the Prime Minister has turned his back on all five. Like the witches in Macbeth, the Prime Minister has had a look at them and does not like the looks of any of them. He dismissed the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador from his Cabinet. He found him not to be of sufficient calibre to be in his Cabinet. The Prime Minister has found no replacement since he appointed, for the ten days that shook the world, the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons). He has found, since then, that the other three are not desirable, either; not of sufficient quality to be in his Cabinet. Imagine, not one of the five Liberal Members in this House from Newfoundland could even be Minister of Fitness and Amateur Sport. Not one of them is fit to be Minister of Fitness and Amateur Sport, not to mention "le ministre des peches". Not one of them is suited to be Minister of Fisheries. Not one of them, apparently, is suited to be Minister of Mines. Not one of them could bear the responsibilities of being a minister without portfolio. The Prime Minister will not even give one of them a portfolio. He will not give them nothing; no way. And the people of Newfoundland are suffering as a result.
We see that today, when we notice facts like these. In constant dollar terms, DREE expenditures in the Atlantic region fell by 41.4 per cent from 1970-71 to 1977-78, while elsewhere in Canada DREE spending rose 5.9 per cent. That is complete political prostitution of the whole program to over-
November 17, 1983

come regional disparity. For the Atlantic provinces which suffer from that regional disparity, spending has fallen 41 per cent, while elsewhere in Canada, in Quebec and other politically important areas, the spending has gone up 5.9 per cent. We need a Cabinet Minister from Newfoundland to stop that kind of discrimination, that kind of twisting of the DREE program for political purposes.
Is the Prime Minister going to appoint a Cabinet Minister from Newfoundland? Are we all waiting with bated breath to see what happens in a certain court case-which shall be nameless-on December 2? Is there not one of the other three Hon. Members who has the pristine purity to be appointed to the Cabinet now? What is to happen if the results in early December are not as the Prime Minister would like them to be? Are we to continue for the next year or year and a half without a Cabinet representative from Newfoundland?
Why is it, for example, the International Centre for Ocean Development was just established in Halifax rather than in St. John's, which is the natural home for it? St. John's is the whole centre of the North Atlantic, and the most suitable area, with the best facilities for an International Centre for Ocean Development. But instead of that, it now resides in Halifax.
Nova Scotia has two Ministers in the Government. One of them is at present hopping with the kangaroos in Australia, the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan). The other is in the House here, but we cannot understand what he is saying in any event. He is a bafflegabber. However, he has a lot of respect, apparently, and power within the Government. Nova Scotia has two Ministers; Newfoundland has none. When are the backbenchers on the Liberal side going to rise up against this and persuade the Prime Minister that he should stay at home, look after the backyard and see that Newfoundland gets some kind of equal and fair treatment in this House? When will the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin), a young man with his future still very much in his past, put a stop to the way the Prime Minister is treating the Province of Newfoundland? When is he going to tell the Prime Minister to stay home and bring peace to Canada before he attempts to bring it to the rest of the world? When is he going to make an effort to solve our domestic problems here in Canada? We have unemployment at 19 per cent and the Prime Minister is going to spend all his time in the next three weeks in Bangladesh and Southeast Asia dealing with the problems of the Commonwealth and the world. Soon he will be dealing with the problems of the universe. There is no problem he cannot deal with, as long as it lies in the ethereal realm outside Canada, outside the real world and outside of helping the real people. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I ask the Prime Minister or his assistant to appoint a Minister from Newfoundland quickly and do something to help with the desperate situation in that Province.

subtopic: PUBLIC WORKS-LEASING OF DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS BUILDING
PUBLIC WORKS-LEASING OF DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS BUILDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find that a hard act to follow, particularly that of the young man who claims he has visions.
I wish to extract some information from the Government on the subject of the lease arrangement for the new DVA Building in Charlottetown. On November 4 I posed a question to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc) on the subject. He was unable to respond at the time but assured me he would

November 17, 1983
Adjournment Debate
look into the matter and write to me directly. To date the Minister has not done so. Perhaps this debate will elicit some response to my original question, which was:
Can the Minister indicate to the House the cost of leasing the DVA Building from Rampart Enterprises during the term of the lease which is, I understand, for 35 years?
I also requested that the Minister table in the House the leasing agreement. Since then I have tabled a notice of motion demanding that these papers be tabled.
The saga of the DVA building in Charlottetown is a long one and it seems to be getting longer. A claim was made by this Liberal Government when it decided in 1980 to move the building to a site in downtown Charlottetown from the shoreline site which had been chosen by the Conservatives that construction would be faster downtown. The Minister of Veterans Affairs at that time said that the building would be completed by the end of 1983. The building is now supposed to be ready by the Spring of 1984.
The construction of that building was supposed to follow one pattern, but has followed quite a different one. It was supposed to be completed in two phases. Phase one was the foundation and superstructure of the building. It was to be constructed for the Department of Public Works through tendered bids. The cost of that phase was $2.8 million and was completed in December of 1981.
Phase two took off in a different direction and tenders were let for the completion of the building by a developer who would construct and own the building and lease it back to the federal Government. This is a very strange way for the Department of Public Works to go about constructing government buildings. Rampart Enterprises of Toronto received the contract to complete the building. Under this arrangement Rampart is given title to the building and Public Works leases it for use by the Veterans Affairs Department over a term of some 35 years. The federal Government also has the opportunity of purchasing the building from the developer at some point during or at the end of the lease.
Some clarification is needed on a number of points of this agreement. What are the exact terms of the lease to purchase contracts? What is the annual cost of the lease? How much will the Government have paid by the time it purchases the building? All this information should be made available to the House of Commons as soon as possible.
When the Supplementary Estimates came out a few days ago I had hopes that we would be able to extract this information from either the Department of Veterans Affairs or Public Works during the committee meetings on those Supplementary Estimates. I have yet to hear from the Chairman of that committee, the Hon. Member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras), who I thought would be in touch with me by now to see when we could arrange to have the committee meetings of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs.
I hope that the Minister's representative will tonight be able to answer some of these questions. If he is not, I hope that he
will urge his Minister to reply to me as he promised to do in the House of Commons on the November 4, providing me with the details of the very unusual method that has been set in motion to construct the DVA building in Charlottetown.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-CIaude Malepart (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: PUBLIC WORKS-LEASING OF DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS BUILDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to answer the question put by the Hon. Member to the Minister responsible for Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc) on November 4 of this year, concerning the cost of leasing the DVA Building located in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, and owned by Rampart Enterprises.
It is important to remember the facts. On April 25, 1982, the Minister of Veterans Affairs announced that a new building intended to house the central administration services of the Department would be built on property belonging to the Canadian Government and located on the corner of Kent and Grafton in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island. In December 1981, the first stage of the project, which consisted in the construction of foundations and the concrete structure, was finished as a project carried out by the Crown.
In April 1982, Public Works Canada proceeded to let tenders for the construction of the rest of the building, according to the lease-to-purchase formula. So that the Department could assess all tenders on the same basis, bidders w'ere asked to tender their bids on the basis of a 17 per cent interest rate for financing.
Among the five builders who tendered bids, Rampart Enterprises made the lowest offer. With a financing rate of 17 per cent, Rampart's bid worked out to $191 per square meter for the first five years of the 35-year lease. These figures will be adjusted when the building is completed, taking into consideration the current Government of Canada rate for five to ten-year bonds.
Mr. Speaker, the building is expected to be completed and ready to receive its occupants by the beginning of 1984. Since interest rates have dropped considerably since tenders were let, it is now estimated that the annual rent over the first five-year period of the lease will be $150 per square meter. As for the rest of the lease, the annual rent will be adjusted upwards or downwards, depending on financing costs for each subsequent period.
Mr. Speaker, regarding the last part of the Hon. Member's question, I can inform him that the Department would be glad to table in the House the complete leasing agreement between the Crown and Rampart Enterprises or to make a copy of it available to interested Members.
November 17, 1983

AGRICULTURE-STABILIZATION PROGRAM SOUGHT FOR BEEF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening I want to talk about a beef stabilization program for Canada. On September 15, 1983, i put a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) asking him what progress was being made by the Department of Agriculture in the negotiations with the provincial Governments to establish a red meat stabilization program which would cover not only beef but pork as well. I understand that some progress has been made on this in the last few weeks but 1 would like to urge upon the Minister and the Department of Agriculture the importance of the red meat industry to the rural parts of our country.
During the past two years there has been essentially no increase in the price of beef cattle for the cow-calf operators, many of whom are in the Algoma and Manitoulin area and produce a significant percentage of the production in the Ontario region.
1 want to quote briefly from a letter I received from Mr. Allen McKenzie, a beef producer in my constituency, from Tehkummah, Ontario. He says:
I am writing about our concerns of the farming industry in Ontario particularly the cow-calf farmer of which we are one.
1 believe Ontario is the only Province without a program to subsidize the cow-calf man and it is here where the cattle industry all starts. Without us, there are no feeder cattle. What happens if we all go out of business because of low prices? One very startling fact is this: in 1973 we received an average price for our calves of 65 cents per pound.
In 1983-ten years later-we received an average price of 75 cents per pound. Can you imagine a 10-cent per pound increase in ten years? You figure the percentage increase in our income for this period and then think of the percentage increase of all our feed, seed and machinery which we have to purchase and tell me how a farmer is to keep going.
What percentage of increased income do most Canadians receive in one year? I'll tell you it is more than the one per cent that we have got for the last ten years.
I should point out that he has a herd of 35 stock cows, and the average increase in income over that ten-year period has only been $245 per year gross.
He concludes:
Do you not feel from this example that something needs to be done now? We sure do. We must remember that the cattle industry starts with us and without us where would we be. Thank you for your time.
I sent a copy of that letter to the Minister of Agriculture in order to make him aware of the desperate plight that faces much of rural Canada, especially those parts of our country which depend on the beef industry.
As I pointed out earlier, the actual returns are something like 25 per cent or 30 per cent less now than they were four years ago and, as Mr. McKenzie points out in his letter, there has been barely a ten-cent per pound increase average for cow-calf operators during the past ten-year period.

As an indication of that plight 1 think we only have to look at the general downgrading that has taken place in rural parts
Adjournment Debate
of our country that depend on the beef industry. There are other sectors like the dairy industry and so on which have administered prices, or prices established by a formula, that are relatively more successful. But clearly for the beef industry some stabilization, some marketing program has to be put in place. I understand that the Ministers of at least four provinces met this year during July, August and October-1 believe they met even more recently-and are in agreement at this stage, but that a final decision and agreement has not been reached.
I would like to urge upon the Minister and the Parliamentary Secretary the importance of making a tripartite agreement very soon. I understand a tripartite agreement is what is being considered among the beef producers, the producing provinces and the federal Government. I think it is significant, as I understand the negotiations to date, that the four Provinces which have shown an interest in participating in the tripartite agreement represent over 80 per cent of the beef production in Canada.
If we look at the dairy industry we find stabilization payments of over $300 million. If we look at crop insurance, we find stabilization of $145 million. If we look at other forms of stabilization provided, for instance, in the grain industry, we find $140 million. In the federal budget there is $1,292 million for the entire budget of the Department of Agriculture, $682 million of which is for stabilization programs.
We are not just talking about assisting a few beef producers, we are talking about a large number of people. We are talking about that important sector of agriculture which really forms the backbone of many of our agricultural communities. I want to urge upon the Minister of Agriculture and his provincial colleagues, of which the Minister of Agriculture for Ontario is one, the urgency of establishing a stabilization program that is fair to the country, and fair to these valuable producers so that they may continue to operate in Canada and produce this valuable food for the consumers.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Bossy (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-STABILIZATION PROGRAM SOUGHT FOR BEEF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) I would like to respond to the question raised by the Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) on the progress being made toward a new red meat stabilization program for beef producers.
By way of background, the Ministers of Agriculture from four Provinces, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, agreed on the general principles of a new stabilization program at the time of the federal-provincial Ministers meeting in Prince Edward Island in June. A task force was established, including representatives from these four Provinces and the federal Department of Agriculture.
After a series of meetings, a draft plan was established for cow-calf producers, slaughter cattle, hogs and lamb. On October 31, the federal Minister of Agriculture chaired a meeting in Ottawa, at which time three of the Provinces agreed to the principle features of these plans. The Manitoba Minister of Agriculture did not attend that meeting, but indicated it was

because of a prior personal commitment and not because he was no longer in support of a national program.
The Provinces that have agreed account for the majority of red meat production in Canada, and consultations are proceeding on the basis of the October 31 agreement.
The Governments involved have decided not to release the details of the plans at this time because they are changing as consultations proceed. Yesterday, representatives from the four Provinces and the federal Government discussed the proposed beef plans with the Canadian Cattlemen's Association. This morning they met with the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. This afternoon they met with the Canadian Pork
Council. Tonight they are meeting with the Canadian Sheep Council.
In addition, arrangements are being made for meetings with the provinces that have not yet agreed to the principles of the new red meat stabilization program. If all goes well in these consultations the new, improved program could be in place by 1984.
